" This is a...departure. Everyone please move aside, because Kris Jenner has arrived on the 2019 Met Gala red carpet—only you'd barely know it, because she legit looks nothing like herself. As we all know, Kris is known for her short black hair. Buuuut not only did she wear a bob for the First Monday in May, she went platinum. Kris' new beauty look presumably was her attempt at ""camp,"" which is the theme of this year's Met Gala. And if you're wondering why she didn't show up in a tent, that's because the theme isn't camping. It's based on Susan Sontag’s 1964 essay titled ""Notes on 'Camp,'"" in which she mused ""the essence of Camp is its love of the unnatural: of artifice and exaggeration."" A blonde wig definitely counts as artifice and apparently was Kylie Jenner's idea, who told Kris, ""mom, there's no black hair tonight—you're going blonde."" Meanwhile, Kris' giant be-winged ""opera coat"" by Tommy Hilfiger is just as about as extra as it gets. Kris told E! she was ""channeling David Bowie"" and that this is how she dressed all through the '80s, FYI. I continue to stan a legend, bye! From: Cosmopolitan US

" Fashion as a tall woman is a minefield Picture this: I'm shopping for holiday outfits for a girls' trip and find the perfect jumpsuit for the occasion. Sadly though, a regular jumpsuit from the high street on a 6'2"" frame means one thing, and one thing only; camel toe. And the next one I try isn't much better. This time, my long arms and 36-inch legs are the problem, leaving me resembling Shawn Wayans from the shopping scene in White Chicks, bursting out of my clothes. Comical, perhaps, but not the look I'm going for. The fact is, shopping on the high street is hard for a tall girl - and it doesn't appear to be getting any better. As brands appear to be streamlining their in-store offerings and prioritising mainlines only (Topshop recently removed their tall section from their Westfield Stratford store and it's an equally uninspiring situation for curvy shoppers, too), anyone outside of the industry-assumed 'standard', is forced to shop online. ""All women should have the luxury of trying before we buy"" ""It’s extremely frustrating, Youtuber Gifty Appiah who runs a Tall Girl Haul tells Cosmopolitan UK, ""but that’s the reality of being 6ft and trying to find clothes that fit.” While some brands do it well - we're looking at you, ASOS Tall - not many of the high street's tall ranges are very inspiring. Think: basic T-shirts, jeans and jackets, don't expect to find that cute playsuit from the mainline collection here! It's frustrating, and something I believe needs to change. All women should have the luxury of trying before we buy. I mean, it would be nice to walk in a store and pick up a cute jumper without having to roll up the sleeves, or to find a pair of trousers that don’t fit like ankle grazers. But alas. While we wait, I hope these tips I've picked up along the way can help you navigate the high street a little easier... Struggle: The sleeves are too short. Solution: Roll them up! I do this all the time, because I refuse to let my long arms limit my fashion choices. This hack also works with with thin knits, blazers and long-sleeve tops. Struggle: They barely cover my bum. Solution: Head straight to ASOS Tall as they usually have a variety of cute mini dresses. Alternatively, buy a midi dress that you like and get it tailored. Yes, it's a longer process. but the outcome always makes it worthwhile. Struggle: I don't want to spend too much money. Solution: Unfortunately, we tall girls don't have the privilege of heading to Primark, chucking a pair jeans in our basket and heading to the tills. When it comes to jeans, knowing your measurements makes the whole process much easier. I know many 5'11 girls who can buy their jeans in H&M and Zara *cries in I 'm 6'2 and this does not apply to me*. For my 6'0 + girls I recommend Topshop Tall jeans. Struggle: All the ones I see look too short. Solution: The key word here is 'look'. A lot of the time us tall girls go into shops and just assume that all the shorts and skirts will be too short for us, when sometimes this really isn't the case. Don't just look, try them on - you might be surprised with the outcome. Struggle: I can't find one that actually fits. Solution: I don't know what it is with sports brands assuming that all women are 5'7 and under but it's almost impossible to find a tracksuit that caters to us tall girls in the women's section. That's why I head straight to the mens department. Men's tracksuits usually fit much better, as there not as tight and restricting as the women's ones - and they cater to our long legs so it's a win/win situation!

" A guide to getting the right bra When was the last time you went for a bra fitting? If the answer is more than six months ago, there's a good chance you could do with booking in another appointment with someone who can help guide you. Fact is, most of us just don't pay enough attention to our underwear drawers. Suzanne Pentland, a bra fitter for Freya and Fantasie, told Cosmopolitan UK that 80% of women are wearing the wrong-sized bra. But, really, why does it matter? ""A correctly-fitting bra reduces breast, upper back and shoulder pain, reduces breast ligament from stretching and breast from dropping, and will stop the underwire from digging into your breast tissue,"" Suzanne explained. So yeah, probably gonna want to make sure you get that right. According to Suzanne, here's what you should be looking for as a bare minimum when it comes to trying on a bra: · Straps sitting comfortably on the shoulders · Brand fitted and sitting correctly under the bust (Band fits firm but comfortable) · Breasts look and feel supported · No overspill in the cup · Underwire sits flat against your chest wall and behind breast tissue · Underband sits parallel all around the body As someone that spent five years working for a department store as a bra fitter, I'd like to think I know a thing or two about bras, and the boobs that fill them. I fitted hundreds - probably thousands - of women, and although they were all different (hence why everyone needs to be fitted individually), I saw many common themes from the customers I worked with. Here's everything I wish every person with boobs knew about finding the right bra: The underband is what will give you most of your support. Too loose, and it'll just ride up and stop you from getting the lift you need. Too tight, and it'll be painful. Of course, there are exceptions, but the one thing I found time and time again when I was doing fittings is that women tend to wear a bigger band size than they need to... whether that's for comfort, to avoid 'back roll' or simply because they just don't know what the right size should feel like. I'd meet women who insisted they were a 40DD, only to find out that they're more like a 38F. And petite, size 6 women would regularly come to me thinking they should be wearing a 36 band. Uh uh honey. If you really can't be doing with a tight underband, why not try a bralette instead? Lingerie brands have clocked on to the fact that comfort is key for many of us, and they're now available in a range of sizes with actual, proper support. WE EARN A COMMISSION FROM PRODUCTS PURCHASED THROUGH SOME LINKS IN THIS ARTICLE. BUY NOW Bralette, £21, Freya @ Figleaves Look, just like a good pair of jeans, you can't just whack on any old bra and expect it to give you a great shape. Some people spend years convinced they need padding, only to try a cotton-cup bra and feel like a new woman. Others might think they look best in a t-shirt bra, but be amazed once they see the lift they can get from a push-up version. My advice? Try 'em all. Sorry, but there's no one-size-fits-all option for bras. Take a padded design, for example; you're probably going to need to size up in the cup, and same goes for a plunge style (if you want to avoid the four-boob look). But if you want a fuller, balcony-style bra, you might even get away with a smaller cup size. Honestly, it's a minefield. Make friends with the store's bra fitter - you're going to need them. BUY NOW Full-cup T-shirt bra, £16, M&S Considering the above tip ^^, it makes total sense to try a bra before you take it home. Sure, it can be a pain to strip off in a badly-lit changing room, but it's better than trawling your purchase all the way home, only to find it gapes or bulges. If you only try one thing before you buy, make it your bra. I've spent hours in the fitting room with one woman before now. Sure, some people are easy - they get measured, and the first style they try on fits. But others need to work on it. Don't go for a fitting when you're in a rush, as it's very likely to be a frustrating process with no helpful conclusion. People tend to gravitate towards fastening their bra on the middle hook, but when it's new you should actually fasten it on the loosest. This is because it will inevitably stretch as you wash it, so then you can get tighter and get plenty of wear out of your purchase. Your straps are also v. v. important. They should be adjusted regularly; the right fit will have enough room for you to slip two fingers underneath, but not so loose that they fall off your shoulders. When you first put your bra on, scoop your boobs into the cups and let them settle. When you lean forward, they shouldn't be falling out. BUY NOW Satin balconette bra, £36, Boux Avenue It's amazing how many people think a properly-fitting bra should be uncomfortable. In fact, it should be the opposite. While you'll definitely notice it's there by the end of the day, there's no way a bra should leave deep indentations, dig into your ribs or restrict your breathing. If this happens, you need a different size or style. See you in six months. Follow Abbi on Instagram.

" Hattie spent years trying to fit into the smallest clothes, before realising she could love fashion and embrace her natural size I remember standing in New Look in the summer of 2014 trying on clothes in front of the changing room mirror. I’d picked out a blue top and a tartan mini skirt; both quite tight. I looked in the mirror and wanted to cry. All I could see was my flaws. I couldn’t stop thinking how awful I looked. That I was too big for the clothes. That I wasn’t skinny enough to wear them. I was a size six. I put back the clothes, and walked out of New Look wearing the baggy t-shirt and leggings I’d walked in with. I remember I’d picked the clothes because they were a size six. I refused to buy anything bigger. I had severe body dysmorphia, to the point where I would look in the mirror and see my body as four times’ bigger than it actually was. It started after I developed bulimia at the age of 16. I was overweight while at school and would get called ‘tree trunk legs’ by the boys who bullied me for my thick thighs. In the space of a year, I ended up losing three stone. My family and friends would tell me I looked too thin, but I never believed them. I convinced myself they were just telling me that to make me feel better about my body. ""I refused to buy anything bigger than a size six"" I would scroll through Instagram and see beautiful, slim girls wearing all the fashion I loved - high waist jeans, crop tops, small skirts, showing off their beautiful bellies and slim legs. And though my body could fit into these things, my eyes saw something different. Buying clothes was a huge issue for me. I would scroll through clothing websites, attempting to avoid the changing mirror ordeal, and I would see so many things I liked. But I would convince myself that they wouldn’t look good on me. Sizing was a very important issue to me, too. If there wasn’t any size sixes left - a size my ill mind convinced me was the only acceptable one to be - I wouldn’t buy something. Because labels to me were a deal-breaker. Being anything bigger triggered me into thinking I was too big. That I needed to lose weight. I would have rather had worn something I didn’t like so much as long as it was a size six, than wear a size bigger in something I loved. Which meant, ultimately, I never truly got to indulge in the fashion I fell in love with. ""Sizing wasn’t just a number to me. It was everything"" Sizing wasn’t just a number to me. It was everything. I would fit my diet around staying a size six. I would exercise to stay a size six. I would squeeze myself into whatever I could to fit a size six. But everything changed in 2015 - when a near-death experience forced me to love my body. In January 2015 I was admitted to hospital with suspected appendicitis. But having my appendix removed didn’t cure my symptoms. A week later, my bowel started to perforate. I was 20 minutes from dying. I was living with ulcerative colitis: a form of inflammatory bowel disease which had actually resulted in me being underweight. I had my large intestine removed and I was given a stoma bag. I remember looking down at my stomach and hating myself. Imagine a young, severely body-conscious girl waking up with a bag attached to her stomach. It killed me. And the first six weeks of recovery was horrible. I couldn’t look at the bag, let alone in the mirror. I would cover my body with the baggiest clothes I could find just so that I didn’t even have to look at the shape of it. But another month later and something suddenly clicked in me. My stoma bag had saved my life. My body had fought to keep me alive. So why did I hate it so much? Why was I constantly punishing it? It was in this moment that I vowed to change. I shouldn't be despising my body. I should be appreciating it; thanking it for saving my life. ""For the first time, I was looking at my body and appreciating it"" I remember the first thing I did was go online to buy some new clothes. And instead of focusing on the sizes, I focused on what I actually liked. I bought a beautiful black skort and a stripy crop top - something I hadn’t worn in a long time. My stoma bag forced me to order a bigger size so that I was comfortable. I remember buying an eight. A voice in my head told me it was bad, but I pushed it to the back of my brain. It was more important to comfort my body than it was to restrict it. When the clothes arrived I tried them on in front of the mirror, and I fell in love with myself. For the first time, I was looking at my body and appreciating it. From that moment on, I indulged in fashion. I’d spent so long buying items that didn’t speak to me just to hide my body away, that I wanted to go all-out and experiment with different items. I’d scroll through Instagram and see influencers looking amazing in different clothes, and instead of thinking ‘that would look awful on me’ I thought about how wonderful it would look. I bought piece after piece, and I didn’t care about the sizes anymore. I bought on the basis of what I thought would look nice and comfortable. And the less I thought about sizes, the more I didn’t care. The longer I stopped looking at the labels on my clothes, the less I thought about them, and the easier it got. The more I looked at myself in the mirror wearing the clothes, instead of looking at the numbers of them, the more I realised that it’s how I looked in the clothes that matters - not what labels, that absolutely nobody can even see, say. After having my bowel removed I started to put on weight, because I was healthier. And not focusing on clothes sizes stopped me focusing on being skinny. I started nourishing my body. I no longer forced it to conform to a size six. Now I'm a size 12, and I've never been happier in my body. I no longer buy clothes for my body to fit into - I buy clothes to fit me. My love fashion has only increased, and my wardrobe is now filled with glorious dresses, crop tops and jeans I never had the guts to wear before. Having a stoma bag may have been traumatic at first, but it forced me to love my body. It forced me to accept and appreciate myself for who and what I am. And what I love the most? That it allowed me re-explore my love of fashion. Follow Hattie on Twitter.

" How to break in new sandals, stop your flip flops from rubbing and keep your feet in tip top condition this summer... Breaking in new shoes can be a painful affair, so how do you go about stopping shoes from rubbing? Flip flops, sandals, strappy high heels – all these summer favourites can wreak havoc on the condition of our feet – and considering they're most exposed at this time of year, it can lead to quite distressing situations. Thankfully, with these summer footwear hacks you and your toes can be in a happy place this season… If you have to wear closed shoes for work… and they get hot or sweaty, put them into a carrier bag and in the freezer overnight. This will kill all bacteria that can cause problems such as fungal infections, says Heidi Meckler MSc, HCPC registered Podiatrist for Strive Footwear. Choose wedges over stilettos where possible… as these offer more support under foot, Heidi says. If you do insist on wearing six inch heels… try spraying some deodorant or applying some vaseline to the inside of the heel area to help avoid blisters, Heidi says. Learn how to walk PROPERLY in high heels… and we don't mean just perfecting walking without falling over. One of the main reasons high heels are painful on the balls of the feet is because all of our body weight is thrown onto the small joints of our toes. Standing up straight and concentrating on putting the weight through your heels will give you immediate relief from the balls of your feet, Heidi says. And if rubbing does occur… make sure you have some surgical tape with you to apply to any areas that begin to rub – it'll prevent blisters and won't cost you an arm and a leg, Heidi says. Choose well-supported sandals over flip flops… flip flops can have a negative impact on your feet, posture and body so ditch them in favour of a more supportive, well-fitting sandal to avoid longer-term problems, Heidi says. But if you're a flip flop fanatic… look for styles which contour towards the bottom of the foot with a thicker strap to hold the foot in place, and avoid thin soles, Heidi says. Hairspray can help your flip flops from sliding… it won't completely prevent slippages from occurring, but will help your grip. Use an old toothbrush to clean the flip flop grooves… bacteria and sweat can build up on the bed of your flip flops and begin to smell, beat this with some water mixed with alcohol and an old tooth brush. If your feet are naturally pongy… socks and sandals are IN right now. Make the most of it. Waterproof your espadrilles… because as gorgeous as they are – canvas shoes and the unpredictable British summer weather are NOT a great mix. Water = damp feet which can lead to infection and nasty smells. If your sandals do get damp… sprinkle some baby powder into your shoes and let them soak up all that horrible moisture. If your stilettos give you dry or cracked heels… try rubbing them twice a week with a foot file and apply Vaseline after a bath. Follow by putting on a pair of cotton socks to allow the Vaseline to soak in, Heidi says. Wear in your shoes before you wear them… by heating up some thick socks with a hairdryer, putting them on inside the shoes and walking around the house in them. Brand new shoes? Use some sandpaper on the soles to give you a better grip.

" It's been in the royal family for a long time Kate Middleton will one day become Queen consort. And while we hope that day will be way, way in the future, there's a significant chance we'll see Prince William take the role of King in our lifetimes. And when that happens, the royal family's website states that Kate will be crowned alongside William, saying ""unless decided otherwise, a Queen consort is crowned with the King, in a similar but simpler ceremony."" This statement is echoed by Paul Burrell, Princess Diana's former butler who told Us Weekly.“Kate will be crowned alongside William at his coronation in Westminster Abbey. “She’ll be crowned queen consort, much in the same way the Queen Mother was [to Queen Elizabeth II’s father, George VI.]” And of course, every Queen needs a crown. In the Duchess' case, it seems likely that it'll be the one that once belonged to the Queen Mother. The stunning crown was created by the then-royal jeweller, Garrard & Co. in 1937 for Queen Elizabeth, and is decorated with around 2800 diamonds - the most notable being the 105-carat Koh-i-Noor diamond in the middle of the front cross. The diamond was first presented given to Queen Victoria in 1856 by the Sultan of Turkey. Upon Victoria’s death the stone became part of the Crown Jewels and has been used on a number of crowns including that of Queen Alexandra and Queen Mary. It was transferred to the Queen Mother's crown It was so important to her that it was placed on top of her coffin during her funeral in 2002. The crown has been on display with the Crown Jewels in the Jewel House at the Tower of London since the Queen Mother's death, and is likely to remain there until it's ready to be used again. Follow Abbi on Instagram.

However, ASOS is also focusing on sustainability going forward, and a part of that means keeping returns to a minimum - meaning those who are taking advantage of the policy may get caught out. The brand explained: The website explains further: ""If we notice an unusual pattern of returns activity that doesn’t sit right: e.g. we suspect someone is actually wearing their purchases and then returning them or ordering and returning loads – way, waaay more than even the most loyal ASOS customer would order – then we might have to deactivate the account and any associated accounts."" Earlier this year, it was reported that brands would 'blacklist' customers who return repeatedly. At the time, ASOS told Cosmopolitan UK that they would only check up on customers if a fraud is suspected, which relates to a very small percentage of shoppers and is normal procedure for online retailers. So that basically means that those who return honestly - i.e. simply because the item doesn't fit, isn't quite right etc. - won't be affected. " LIFE-CHANGING. We all know the pure hell that is shopping for a new pair of jeans. There's a reason why most women feel something akin to grief when a brand discontinues their favourite style. Once you find them, it's just easier all-round to stick to what you know, right? But for me, jeans shopping has been so awful - so properly traumatic - that I basically stopped doing it when I was a teenager. Jeans have just never been a part of my wardrobe and I know why... Aside from the fact that I do love dresses and skirts, I've never managed to find denim to fit properly. Not cheap, high street jeans, not expensive brands. Nada. If we're doing that thing that people always insist we do, where we compare women's bodies to fruit (UGH), I'd be like... an extreme pear. By which I mean my waist is relatively small in comparison to my bum, hips and legs. Which doesn't tend to bode well for denim; even that of the stretchy kind. Please don't think that this is me complaining about my body. Just like any woman, years of shopping and near-breakdowns in fitting rooms have taught me to appreciate what I've been blessed with. One of the benefits of being a fashion editor and constantly staring at clothes, is that I tend to know at first glance whether something will suit me. I'm tall, so midi skirts and dresses get a big tick. Case in point, these bathroom selfies: Your fave librarian 👋🏻 #hohselfiemirror A post shared by Abigail Malbon (@abbimalbon) on Mar 6, 2019 at 10:06am PST Spring mode activated (temporarily, probably) #hohselfiemirror A post shared by Abigail Malbon (@abbimalbon) on Feb 21, 2019 at 1:14am PST Tailored trousers and jeans absolutely do not suit me. That's just the way it's always been. That is, until I was browsing the high street recently and came across a pair of jeans in & Other Stories that I thought *might* just fit me. They had all the makings of a flattering pair: wide legs (but still tapered, I'm so over being confined to culottes), a high waist, a self-tie belt and a nice, thick material that wouldn't chafe away after three wears. Spoiler alert: I bought them. And - this is not an exaggeration - they have changed my life. I never have any expectations when I try jeans on. Actually, that's a lie. I expect to put them straight back on the shop floor. But these were a revelation. Not only did they fit, they were comfortable and flattering. They fitted loosely on the calves (this never happens) and didn't gape on my waist. So, I went back for more. I wanted to know whether these excellent, comfortable jeans were an anomaly, or if & Other Stories is truly my high street saviour. I bought a second pair, this time black, high-waisted stretch kickflares...and guess what? THEY FIT. Now, I'm not saying every single pair in the store will be the same. I fully intend to stay in my lane, and that lane does not include: a. skinny or b. straight-leg styles. But just knowing that I have the option of throwing on a pair of jeans and a t-shirt is liberating. I wasn't even scared about how to style them. I was READY. Since investing, been able to wear things that I really struggled to wear before: a long blazer, a square-neck buttoned-up blouse, ruffled tops that would have been too voluminous to pair with a full midi skirt. Dresses will always be my first love - and the reason I'm living on beans by the end of every month - but it truly feels like a relief to have jeans that fit. " The brand made a statement following the Leaving Neverland documentary Louis Vuitton has said that it will not produce the Michael Jackson pieces that appeared in its autumn/winter 2019 menswear show, following the airing of the Leaving Neverland documentary. The programme interviews two men who accuse the pop star of having sexually abused them as children. The documentary was first aired on 25 January at Sundance, the week after Louis Vuitton presented its menswear show on 17 January. Jackson references included a T-shirt with a graphic of his dancing feet, and styling details such as white socks worn with loafers, statement gloves, sequinned tops and loose white button-up shirts. Creative director Virgil Abloh said at the time that he wanted to ""make a point about the humanity in [Jackson’s] vision"". However, the brand has since said in a statement that the documentary has caused Vuitton ""the greatest pain"" and highlighted that it was unaware of the programme when the menswear collection was presented. “I am aware that in light of this documentary the show has caused emotional reactions. I strictly condemn any form of child abuse, violence or infringement against any human rights,” said Abloh. ""My intention for this show was to refer to Michael Jackson as a pop culture artist. It referred only to his public life that we all know and to his legacy that has influenced a whole generation of artists and designers."" Vuitton chairman and CEO Michael Burke described the allegations as ""deeply troubling and disturbing"". “Child safety and welfare is of utmost importance to Louis Vuitton,"" he said. ""We are fully committed to advocating this cause.” From: Harper's BAZAAR UK

" Tired of never being able to find the clothes she wanted to wear, 27-year-old Jazmin Lee took matters into her own hands. As a woman whose size fluctuates between a 16 and a 20, Jazmin Lee knows all too well just how restrictive the plus-size fashion industry is. Which is why, at just 27 years old, she has been awarded the Prince's Trust Enterprise Award for founding her own inclusive fashion brand. In her own words, Plus Equals, was ""Founded out of the frustration of fierce fashion for fatter femmes"". With sizes ranging from a 14 to 42 (with made to measure items available at no extra cost), Lee has single-handedly proven that there's more to plus size fashion than butterfly printed smock tops. Here's how she turned her pipe dream into a reality, and how she's changing the fashion industry for the better."" Find your niche ""I grew up in a creative household. My Nan, Mum and Grandad were all artists, so they always encouraged me to sew and draw. I've always been into very theatrical fashion, which probably comes from watching Cats on repeat! ""As I grew older, I wanted to continue to be colourful and expressive with my fashion, but I I couldn't fit in any Tammy Girl clothes, which left me with Etam. All I wanted to do was shop somewhere like Punky Fish, but my size meant I was limited to basic, boring, pieces, which didn't reflect my personality. ""In order to express myself I started buying my clothes from charity shops and boots sales. Mixing those pieces with my boring Etam staples gave me the identity I so desperately craved. When Lady Gaga came out I found this new sense of confidence, it sounds cheesy but she is really the one who made me refuse to hide away in boring clothes. ""I was studying for a fashion degree, but getting into the industry is incredibly difficult. I lost my Mum and Nan before the age of 25 and as I was a carer for my Nan, interning just wasn't a possibility for me. I had dreamed of staring my own brand and when my Nan passed away I just thought 'What have you got left to lose?'"" Don't go it alone ""I wrote down all my ideas for Plus Equals, but I didn't know anything about the technical side of running a business: Accounting, marketing, search engine optimisation were all alien terms to me. ""I realised if I was going to make my business a reality, I needed help from someone who had done it before. Which is why I reached out to the Prince's Trust, who not only mentored me, but put me in touch with The Samuel Wilson Loan Trust. I got a £10,000 loan which enabled me to stock up on fabric, equipment, marketing and website design."" Be the change you want to see ""I knew I couldn't do a size 14 to 26 range because that leaves so many people out, and my whole mission was to create positive change in the plus-size industry. I went with the brightest prints, the sparkliest sequins, everything that I wanted to wear on a night out, but hadn't been able to. ""I love David Bowie, Blondie, Grace Jones, all those 80s icons and I want my brand to reflect that. I made the entire range non-binary about a year ago because being as inclusive as possible is the most important thing to me. ""I see it as my responsibility to put images out there that represent everyone, which is why I don't want my models to hide or smooth anything. I just think if you don't want someone as they are, why are you even doing it in the first place? It makes no sense to me. I'm working on a one-person budget, I can't afford to do these big campaigns, but these bigger brands can and they're not. Which is why I put my money into hiring larger models and raising their profiles. ""We need to drop the idea of a 'perfect' plus-size body, instead we need to see a whole array of bodies. We need to see those size ranges growing because if the fashion industry took us more seriously they would be booming. I've managed to price my clothes accordingly so you won't pay any different from a size 14 to 42, these brands that charge more for plus-size clothes are just showing a lack of commitment to our community."" Prepare to work your arse off ""At the moment everything you see on the website is handmade by me, it takes me between seven and ten days to make something for my main ready-to-wear line, but for custom orders it takes longer. That's not taking into account running the website, social channels, marketing, and everything else in between. ""I still keep a part-time job two days a week. The thing no one tells you is that when you first start making money from your business you have to invest it back in to keep going."" Dream big ""My end goal for my brand is to create local jobs for young creators who have struggled, and pay them a fair wage. I want to create social change around how we're seeing bodies, and not just plus-sized women. People of colour, LGTBQ+ communities as well, sod Victoria's Secret. Oh, and dress Lizzo, she's my queen, In 2019 I'm making it my mission to get to her."" Follow Plus Equals on Instagram.

The emerald tiara lent to the bride by the Queen and the groom's black and grey morning suit made by Savile Row tailors, Huntsman, will also be included. Book tickets The special exhibit aims to give visitors a chance to view the detail and craftsmanship involved in the creation of the bride and groom's outfits following their nuptials on 12 October last year. And there's no doubt that Eugenie's dress, with its fitted bodice and full-pleated skirt, is the star of the show. The fabric was created with symbols that are meaningful to the bride and groom, including the White Rose of York and ivy, representing the newlyweds home, Ivy Cottage. Eugenie also requested a low back on the portrait-neckline gown, so that the scar from surgery she underwent aged 12 to correct scoliosis could be seen. In a recording made for visitors, Eugenie explains: ""I had always wanted a low back, part of it was showing my scar. I believe scars tell a story about your past and your future and it’s a way of getting rid of a taboo. For me it’s a way of communicating with people who are going through either similar situations with scoliosis or having a scar of their own they are trying to deal with."" Of course, the display wouldn't be complete without the Greville Emerald Kokoshnik Tiara that the bride borrowed from her grandmother. Originally made in 1919, this will be the first time it has been exhibited in its history. Eugenie's diamond and emerald drop earrings, which were a gift from her new husband, will be featured alongside the impressive headpiece. Also on show is the striking Ralph & Russo maid of honour outfit worn by Princess Beatrice, plus the clothing worn by bridesmaid, Theodora Williams, and pageboy, Louis de Givenchy. Their sweet outfits were made by the London-based children’s designer Amaia Kids. The exhibition comes after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's wedding outfits were shown in Windsor last autumn. This display closed on 6 January, but if you missed seeing Meghan's dress, it will be open at the Palace of Holyroodhouse from 14 June to 6 October 2019. " They've already been fur-free for over a decade Selfridges is the latest fashion brand to ban the use of exotic skins, joining others like Victoria Beckham and Chanel. The luxury department store has vowed to stop selling products made from python, alligator, lizard and crocodile skin by 2020, according to WWD. From February 2020, the department store will only sell leather goods made from agricultural livestock, including cow, sheep, pig, goat, water buffalo and lamb. Claire Bass, executive director at the Humane Society International, told the Guardian: “Banning exotic skins in recognition of the serious animal welfare issues that exist in this industry is a natural next step for a responsible retailer.” For a brighter future | As part of our commitment to Buying Better, Inspiring Change, we will phase out the sale of exotic skins completely by 2020. " So long, washing pile! Okay, hands up if you've ever sheepishly pulled your favourite top out of the wash basket because you've been way too busy to stick a wash on but you obviously still need to wear it (🙋). Turns out that's actually socially acceptable, as long as you have a bottle of dry shampoo for clothes. Because that's now a thing that exists. WIN. Day2 is the world's first dry wash spray, and was created when the inventors discovered that only 40% of the clothes we wash are actually dirty. Instead of sticking another load on, you can refresh your clothes by laying them on a flat surface, spraying, smoothing out and hanging up. The brand claims within 15 minutes your clothes will be softer, smell fresher and look freshly ironed. And it's only £7.50 a can. There's nothing more annoying than washing your jeans and having to play the 'Have I gained weight or do I just need to stretch these back out again?' game, but there's a specific denim spray for that - or you can also buy original or delicate (perfect for winter jumpers you're scared of shrinking). The brand recommends using them for everything from everyday to gym clothes, and while I'd be sceptical about refreshing my top after a sweaty spin class (don't be that person), there's no arguing that the spray is better for the longevity of your wardrobe and good for the environment. As it says on the Day2 website, a bottle of their spray is made with only 0.02% of the water in a normal laundry load - plus it's carbon neutral when sprayed. Just a heads up; the brand doesn't recommend using the product on properly dirty clothes, but if there's no stains? Spray away. Follow Abbi on Twitter.

" The designer was absent from a Chanel couture show last month Iconic fashion designer Karl Lagerfeld has died aged 85, Chanel has announced. The French fashion designer passed away following weeks of ill health. Alain Wertheimer, CEO of Chanel, said: “Thanks to his creative genius, generosity and exceptional intuition, Karl Lagerfeld was ahead of his time, which widely contributed to the House of Chanel's success throughout the world. Today, not only have I lost a friend, but we have all lost an extraordinary creative mind to whom I gave carte blanche in the early 1980s to reinvent the brand.” Bruno Pavlovsky, President of Fashion at Chanel said: “Fashion show after fashion show, collection after collection, Karl Lagerfeld left his mark on the legend of Gabrielle Chanel and the history of the House of Chanel. ""The greatest tribute we can pay today is to continue to follow the path he traced by – to quote Karl – ‘continuing to embrace the present and invent the future’.” The news comes after Lagerfeld missed his end-of-show-bow during the Chanel haute couture show in January. In a statement following the show, Chanel said that the designer was ‘feeling tired’ and ‘asked Virginie Viard, director of the creative studio of the house, to represent him.' It was the first time he had missed an end-of-show bow. Paris Match reports that Karl was hospitalised on Monday night and passed on Tuesday morning. The designer was known as one of the most recognisable faces in fashion due to his white hair, ponytail and dark glasses. He once said of himself: ""I am like a caricature of myself, and I like that."" He has been the creative director of Chanel since 1983, plus creative director of Fendi and his own eponymous fashion label. Fellow designers have been paying tribute to Lagerfeld via social media. " So you find getting dressed in the mornings SO much easier... Let's be honest, wardrobes can be stressful affairs. And no matter how many pieces you own, it's easy to feel like you never have anything to wear. Which is why we've spoken to expert Practical Princess' Elika Gibbs and Virginia Feacey, Country Manager UK at second-hand designer resale site Rebelle, to find out how we can all lead less cluttered lives. 1. Start with one big clear-out Virginia suggests going through every item in your wardrobe and adding to 'SELL', 'MAYBE', 'CUSTOMISE' and 'TOSS' piles. Get more advice on how to start this process and see how I got on with a mass clear-out right here. Elika suggests to try things on as you go ""because you may have forgotten about a missing gem that's been sitting in your wardrobe that you normally bypass. You might be able to alter it to make it more current. 2. And then continuously edit your wardrobe Virginia recommends starting a one-in-one-out policy, to avoid cluttering. ""For every new item you purchase"", she says, ""an old one needs to go. Or, if you really want to test yourself, try two."" Why? Elika tells us, ""If you don't edit your wardrobe, you might think you have loads of clothes but actually, it's just that you have volume of things that no longer fit or are dated. ""By clearing out your wardrobe you prevent that, and you'll find getting dressed in the mornings so much easier."" 2. Make some money with your unwanted bits ""Just because you might not like it anymore, doesn't mean someone else won't!"", Virginia says. ""It’ll also make you feel better if you want to purchase something new, if you're making money from the old"". Use sites like Ebay and Depop for your high street purchases, and ones like Rebelle for more high-end pieces. 3. Organise your closet by category and then by colour ""It’ll make everything look much neater and will save you time in the mornings when you need to get dressed in a hurry"", Virginia advises. 4. Invest in the right equipment ""I like matching hangers because then you're not distracted by a messy wardrobe"", Elika says. And Virginia agrees: ""Get some good hangers with rounded corners and use boxes to keep drawers organised. This is especially great for belts, underwear and socks."" 5. Separate the seasons ""If wardrobe space is an issue"", Virginia says, ""divide your things into summer and winter clothing and keep the other season packed up out of the way"". Elika agrees that this can be handy regardless. ""It's no good if it's the middle of winter and you're going through your closet and you have summer dresses hanging there that you won't be able to wear"", she says. 6. Store everything in the right place ""Keep knitwear folded and flat. Also dry it flat to avoid pulling and deformation"", Virginia says. 7. Don't forget your shoes ""If you have a lot of shoes in boxes"", Virginia says, ""tape pictures of the shoes to the outside of the box, so you know what’s inside without having to go through several boxes."" Elika adds: ""Boxes are ideal because they prevent dust, and cardboard works well because then they can breathe"". 8. And look after more expensive items If you've spent all that money on something fancy, you better make sure you take proper care of it, Virginia says. ""Keep designer bags in their dust bags and stuff them from the inside to avoid deforming."" 1. Invest in good quality wardrobe staples ""These will be the backbone of your wardrobe!"" Virginia tells us. ""You’ll get great cost per wear out of them, so choose pieces that are of good quality, versatile, easily combinable and perhaps a bit pricier, so they’ll last you longer. Think: a good trench or coat, a basic white shirt, a basic cotton Tee, a black blazer, dark blue denim, a cashmere sweater, white trainers, black heels, black flats etc."" 2. Buy into trends with easy to combine and less pricey pieces Love the ruffle trend? Don't splash a load of money on a jumper you'll wear for one season and then throw away. Instead, use the high street for easy trend updates. ""That way it won’t hurt you too much when you stop wearing these pieces"", Virginia says. 3. Take your time before you buy Before you spend any money on something new, Virginia says it's important to consider the purchase first. ""Think of three ways to combine the new piece with existing things in your wardrobe"", she suggests. ""If you don’t come up with three, rethink the purchase."" 4. Always sleep on it ""To avoid impulse buys"", Virginia says, ""research the pieces you need/like, put them on your wish list and then sleep on it. If you still want the pieces the next day, then go ahead and buy them."" 5. Find a great tailor! Can't afford to buy high-end but want your clothes to look more expensive? Virginia says it's all in the way your clothes fit you. ""This means hemming trousers and sleeves, making sure shoulders fit in blazers/ jackets etc"", she says. ""Just make sure you always think about the additional cost of tailoring a piece before you purchase it.""
"

" Truly some ICONIC moments here. The Grammy Awards have had plenty of iconic, classic, and even downright weird fashion moments, but one thing they have in common is that they're all truly memorable. Who could forget J. Lo's plunging Versace number or T. Swift's first-ever Grammys dress? Click through to see the most iconic looks from the awards. Whitney Houston posed with her second Grammy in this abstract black-and-white embellished dress after winning Best Female Pop Vocal Performance for ""I Wanna Dance With Somebody."" She wore black shoes with sparkly details at the ankle and accessorised with silver jewellery. Gloria Estefan wore this shimmery yellow-gold dress with drop earrings to the Grammys, where she was nominated for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance. The singer also took home an award for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance, although one could argue her best vocal performance is ""All I Want For Christmas Is You."" Natalie Cole's ""Unforgettable"" album won every category it was nominated in for a total of three Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year. Here, she posed with an award wearing a spaghetti-strap beaded black and white dress with a neck scarf. Janet Jackson wore a white suit and accessorized with a white headband, a choker, and a red ribbon to raise HIV and AIDS awareness. Annie Lennox channeled her Disney fandom when she wore this pair of Minnie ears on the red carpet along with a patent-leather mini dress and thigh-high boots. Cheryl James (""Salt""), Sandra Denton (""Pepa""), and Deidra Roper (""DJ Spinderella"") — were fresh in their matching mint-green pantsuits and clear handbags. Even their shoes matched. Céline Dion wore no accessories here, letting her brown, crochet halter dress speak for itself. Her voluminous hair, coupled with the extremely sheer gown, made for a bold, memorable look. Aretha Franklin showed up to the Grammys in an all-white ensemble featuring a fur-trimmed collar and hand warmer. It was the year she won the Grammy Hall of Fame Award for her song, ""Respect."" Jada Pinkett Smith wore a beige dress featuring a side cut-out and a leg slit that revealed lace-up heels. She accompanied her husband, Will Smith, who won Best Rap Solo Performance for ""Gettin' Jiggy Wit It."" Jennifer Lopez made this plunging, tropical-printed Versace dress instantly iconic when she wore it to the Grammy Awards in 2000, and it even helped inspire the idea of Google Images. ""At the time, it was the most popular search query we had ever seen,"" said Google executive founder Eric Schmidt. ""But we had no surefire way of getting users exactly what they wanted: JLo wearing that dress. Google Image Search was born."" Destiny's Child wore these green lacy dresses, all of which were made by Beyoncé's mom and the group's costume designer, Tina Knowles. Pink stepped out in this black and pink getup, which could have been taken straight out of the over the top ""Lady Marmalade"" music video. Blige brightened up the red carpet with this neon-yellow outfit. The R&B singer wore a furry coat over her sequined dress and paired it with metallic green heels. Beyoncé was a vision in this silver pleated gown, which she wore the year she won Best Contemporary R&B Album. " The injustice! Let's be honest here; we all love ASOS. We love their Curve collection, we love their beauty buys, we even love the ridiculous things they sell. But most of all, we love how easy they make it to return. Need a new dress for a party? You can order three, and keep the one that looks best (or, in my case, keep all three and spend the rest of the month eating beans on toast). Left gift shopping until the last-minute? No need to worry - just panic-buy and you're bound to find something to suit anyone, and the rest can be returned easily. However, it has been reported that our frivolous shopping habits might soon have consequences - specifically, those who return regularly will be 'blacklisted' by retailers. According to new research conducted by resource planning platform Brightpearl, which asked more than 200 retailers across the UK about their biggest issues, shops have seen a huge increase in returns in recent times. As a result, retailers like ASOS told the survey they are planning to monitor repeat offenders - and have already resorted to checking social media accounts to catch out customers who wear clothes before returning them, according to The Independent. They've also been monitoring those who say they haven't received items they bought. ASOS told Cosmopolitan UK that they would only check up on customers if a fraud is suspected, which relates to a very small percentage of shoppers and is normal procedure for online retailers. Which basically means that those who return honestly - i.e. simply because the item doesn't fit, isn't quite right etc. - won't be affected. PHEW. Follow Abbi on Twitter.

" A woman noticed the new shop has something most others don't: a bridal mannequin in a wheelchair. In a celebratory moment for inclusivity, a woman recently noticed and shared something she's never seen before in a store window: a mannequin modelling a bridal gown, posed in a decorated wheelchair. The display was spotted by Beth Wilson, 36, who is disabled herself. Wilson saw the model in Portishead, Bristol and shared a photo of it on her Twitter so people all over the world could also see and celebrate the rare moment of disability inclusivity in fashion. The new wedding shop in town has a wheelchair using mannequin and it shouldn’t be exciting but it’s the first time I’ve ever seen disability portrayed in a shop window. pic.twitter.com/N5sco2fLJf ""This is the first time I’ve seen a wheelchair in a shop window like this (mobility shops not included) and it was so surprising to see and made me feel represented,"" Wilson says. ""So often disabled people feel invisible because we don’t see ourselves in the media much, and especially not modelling beautiful clothes. The reaction on Twitter has shown that it means a lot to other people, too."" The mannequin is in the window at The White Collection, a bridal boutique in Portishead. Wilson praised the shop for not just including a mannequin in a wheelchair in its display, but for decorating the chair with green vines. ""Mobility aids are often portrayed as negative things that people want to hide when actual mobility aids like wheelchairs give us freedom,"" Wilson says. ""It’s great that the decorated the chair rather than try and hide it away."" The display comes after former basketball Paralympian Zoe was seen searching for her dream dress as a size 24/26 double amputee on TLC show The Curvy Brides Boutique. She said: ""Disabled people do get married too. Look at what you can provide, there are ramps you can buy that actually fold down and can be stored away. If your changing rooms aren't big enough, consider offering appointments when no one else is in the shop for people with wheelchairs."" So while the bridal boutique isn't the first to feature a mannequin using a mobility device like a wheelchair (a JC Penny in New York City had a display including a wheelchair in 2014), as Wilson points out, this sort of inclusivity is exceedingly rare. And if the reaction to her original tweet is any indication, it's something a lot of people would readily welcome and celebrate. Follow Hannah on Twitter. From: Cosmopolitan US

" The pom pom jumper is no longer available Boohoo has been caught for selling a jumper containing real fur, despite advertising it on the site as 'faux'. The fashion brand's 'faux fur pom pom jumper' was sold on the site in September 2018 and was found to contain real fur, likely to be from rabbits. The discovery was made when Humane Society International (HSI) spotted it during an investigation into fur being wrongly labelled in the UK. The jumper was sent to get tested, and it was confirmed that it did contain real fur. HSI then submitted a complaint to the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), which carried out a separate investigation. Boohoo.com told the ASA that they have a ""strong commitment against the sale of real fur in any of their products."" They added that it was their understanding that the item, which was obtained from an external UK-based supplier, was faux, and had been inspected by Boohoo's quality control team. They have since said that they have stopped placing orders with the supplier. The product has been removed from sale, but is currently still on the website. The site's Animal Welfare Policy states that the company is committed to not selling real animal fur. Boohoo told Cosmopolitan UK: An ASA spokesman said: ""Boohoo’s records showed that a sample of fur from the product in question had passed internal tests. ""However, given that we had seen evidence that the product obtained by Humane Society International contained real animal fur, we concluded that the ad was misleading. ""We told Boohoo.com UK not to state that products included “faux fur” if that was not the case."" The investigation also looked into claims that a company called Zacharia Jewellers was selling a product named 'Zac’s Alter Ego Faux Fur Pom Pom Headband’ The headbands, which were purchased from China, have been confirmed as containing rabbit fur. Zacharia Jewellers has since removed the product from its website and from Amazon.

" Handbag cleaning tips for removing stains, scuffs and bringing your leather or material designer handbags back to life... Designer leather handbags are often the one real investment we're willing to make when it comes to the wardrobe department. And, when you've invested a lot of money in a handbag, making sure it's a forever item is a must. But taking care of leather goods can be tricky - and when it's an item you seriously care about, so much more is a stake. So, how do you clean a leather handbag without ruining it? The place to start, says Jordan Smith of the Handbag Clinic, is with prevention. ""Always protect your leather bag with a reputable protection cream/treatment. " A lawsuit has been filed in the U.S. over the ""identical knock-offs"". Vans and its parent company VF Corp are suing Primark for allegedly copying the design of two of their skateboard trainers. The footwear brand claims that the fast-fashion retailer has been selling ""identical knock-offs"" in the U.K. since 2017, WWD reports. Although Vans thought the issue had been settled last January after it asked Primark to stop selling the products, the American trainer manufacturer later discovered that the footwear was on sale in Primark in the U.S. A lawsuit alleging trademark infringement, unfair competition and false advertising was filed in New York last month. The two designs in dispute are the Vans Old Skool sneaker, featuring the iconic side stripe, and the Vans Sk8-Hi sneaker, a lace-up high top also with the classic stripe. The court documents state that Primark's use of a side stripe on its trainers is confusing to the consumer. ""The Side Stripe Trademark’s prominent placement and often-contrasted colour make Vans’ shoes immediately recognisable to consumers even at far-off distances,” say the documents. ""The infringing products are calculated and intentional knock-offs of Vans’ footwear products, and have been designed to confuse the purchasing public."" #cute #pretty #love #vans #van #ilovevans #primark #fakevans #primarkvans A post shared by @ fakevansc on Sep 12, 2018 at 8:14am PDT The lawsuit also references the names used by Primark and highlights that some customers have been calling Primark's trainers as ""fake Vans"" on social media. ""'Skater low tops' and 'Skater high tops' in a blatant attempt to suggest a connection with Vans’ products that bear the Vans trademarks and trade dress, including the Vans’ Old Skool Shoe and Sk8-Hi Shoe,"" state the documents. A representative for Primark told WWD that the company disagrees with the allegations and that they plan to ""defend"" their decision. Cosmopolitan has contacted Primark for comment.

" Mainly: Stop buying light blue jeans I'm often told - by colleagues, family, friends, my boyfriend, my ASOS delivery man - that I own far too many clothes. I don't know what qualifies them to swoop down and officially label my clothing collection as 'too big' but it reached a point when there was just no escaping it any more. I had a problem. Recently, my partner and I moved into our first small house and out of my parents' larger one, where I occupied a large wardrobe and storage in two of the other bedrooms. In our new place, we initially tried to limit our clothes to just the one walk-in wardrobe (we converted the box room into a room for our clothes). I failed miserably and my clothes just spread everywhere. As the new year rolled in, I knew I had to make a change. I was wearing the same clothes to work every week and felt no affection towards my wardrobe whatsoever. Everything was old, or boring, or really 'last season'. The only thing that would make me feel mildly better was buying new clothes, which would just fuel the anger again after a few weeks. I decided to invite an expert in decluttering into my home to see if she could shake me out of my hoarding rut and teach me some organisational tips along the way. Thankfully, Virginia Feacey, Country Manager UK at Rebelle is used to a little bit of closet chaos. As part of her job at the second-hand resale site, Virginia often goes into client's homes to help them identify the diamonds in the rough. Somehow, I thought our experience together might end up a little fruitless. ""I don't own any labels"", I told Virginia almost as soon as she'd walked in the front door. She smiled and told me I'd be surprised at how little I knew about my own clothes, pointing out a pair of UGG boots that I'd left lying on the living room floor. ""That's a label"", she said. Tail between my legs, we went upstairs where I guided Virginia around my various storage spots. To give you a mental image: At any given time, I have three drawers of activewear, jeans and underwear, a rail for my skirts, trousers, tops and knits, and another for my blazers and dresses in the walk-in. There's also a closet in our spare room which houses my coats and bags, one bigger drawer in our bedroom where my nightwear and loungewear live and then my shoes are just all over the house in various free spaces I manage to find. And that's only the current season. I keep next season's clothes in a suitcase (or three) on top of my wardrobe and have another large case for my skiwear. Yes, I have a problem and no, I'm not proud of it. ""Let's get started!"" Virgina said, more enthusiastically than I would have felt in her shoes. We started by created four piles labelled with: 'SELL', 'MAYBE', 'CUSTOMISE' and 'TOSS'. Clothes were then sorted into these piles according to these rules. TOSS: Throw anything that is ripped or stained, super dirty or too worn to give away into a big bin liner. SELL: Put everything that you don't want to keep that's still in a good enough condition to sell or is of value in a box. MAYBE: If an item fits and is in a good condition but you simply can’t decide if you like it or not, put it here. Then, hide the box somewhere so you won't see it every day and note if you ever miss any of the items. ""If you completely forget about them it's a sure sign that you can get rid of them for good"", Virginia told me. CUSTOMISE: If you have clothes that you really like, that don't fit any more or items with buttons missing or hems that need altering, pop them in this box. But be honest with yourself about taking them to be fixed and make sure the cost of alteration is worth it! Everything else goes back into your wardrobe, organised by 'category' i.e. tops, knits, skirts and then by colour. ""If you want to end up with a tidy closet afterwards, take everything out and really examine each item as you go"", Virginia advised. ""Try anything on that you need to, and sort into the boxes as you go."" Virginia gave me some simple questions to ask myself as we did just that. Does it fit? Have you worn it in the last year? Because if you haven't, you'll probably never wear it again. (Excluding occasion-wear). Does it have a history or special meaning? You should keep it! Find a place outside of your wardrobe to store it, where it won’t get dusty. Does it make you feel good? Does it go with other things in your wardrobe? Is it in good condition? If not, can it easily be fixed or will you actually take it to get fixed? Is it annoying or uncomfortable to wear? Having a relative stranger look through your wardrobe really brings a fresh perspective on your shopping habits. I found myself cringing at showing Virginia some of the items I owned. Odd, considering that I obviously liked them at one point. I also quickly realised that in a few cases I had five versions of the same thing; five sweaters, five light blue pairs of jeans (actually more), and about nine pairs of gym leggings. BUT I only had one 'going out' top and zero pairs of dark blue jeans. Virginia agreed that my wardrobe was missing some of the more 'classic' staples. ""Replace the cashmere knit that shrunk in the wash!"", she told me afterwards. ""And don’t put the next one in the washing machine"". Her other observation? ""Don’t be afraid to throw things out you are no longer wearing or don’t love!"" she told me, nodding her head towards another top I said was a gift and I couldn't throw. ""Of course hang on to things you have an emotional attachment to or good memories of, but just because it was a gift, doesn’t mean you need to hang on to it."" Decluttering expert Marie Kondo preaches that we should only ever buy or keep things that bring us joy. Virginia tried to get me into this mindset when we were trawling through my rails and my piles, and piles of shoes. We ended up finding a lot to chuck - some of which is in a good enough condition to take to the charity shop - and a decent pile that I could sell, too. Among the numerous Topshop striped tops we did find a few gems. A Peter Pilotto co-ord from Target that I never wear, a cute top-of-the-high-street bag and an old pair of Louboutins I think have been on my feet all of one time (because OUCH). It's items like these Virginia says would be great listings on Rebelle while cheaper items can go on Ebay or Depop. Aside from my spanking new, colour-coded, decluttered heaven of a wardrobe?! Since living my new, decluttered life, I'm noticing that I'm wearing clothes I haven't worn in ages. In fact, the first day that I got dressed after the edit, I picked a top I'd forgotten existed because it was buried so deep among everything else. This was another takeaway from the experiment - keeping a tidy wardrobe and drawers will help me see what I have and make dressing in the mornings easier. I honestly feel quite embarrassed about the sheer volume of clothes that I had, and so really want to make a conscious effort not to get that way again. I'm going to try Virginia's one in one out policy, and just try to buy less stuff in general. I've written a list of all the 'staples' my wardrobe seems to be missing, so if I do ever get a shopping urge, it'll be on one of these investment pieces rather than that cute floral, boho, wrap top from Zara. My plan is to try and do a wider edit of my clothes every few months, so that it never feels too overwhelming. We'll see if I stick to it! Overall I found the experience cathartic and cleansing. I actually am excited about my new shopping mindset - and all the space I'm going to gain in my house!

Where should you go? Before doing anything, make sure you find a body piercer who is reputable. Most piercers will have done an apprenticeship, as it is a more self-regulated industry."" Kevin says that at Liberty ""we always suggest to have food beforehand"" and to remember some parlours will require ID if you look under 16, so make sure you have it with you. What's the process? ""We ask customers to come in a little earlier for their appointment to go through the choices of jewellery"", Kevin says. ""Once this has been done and payment has been taken, we sterilise the jewellery to make it safe to put through the body - this takes roughly ten minutes - and then call you through to the piercing room. ""Once you are in the room the piercer will clean your skin and make a mark of where we think is the best placement for your anatomy. While everyone experiences different levels of pain, you should expect to always feel some discomfort. Kevin explains: ""All piercings pinch a little but the procedure is over with very quickly so it's all relative. Should you have a gun or a needle? For Kevin, it's pretty obvious that the needle has the advantage. He says: ""The only pro to a gun is that they are faster. They are not as accurate as a needle and they cannot be fully sterilised, where as all our needles are single use. It's worth thinking a bit about the process, too. ""[With a gun] you are using a sharpened piece of jewellery with force and velocity to break your skin, where a needle is a much smoother process. It may take an extra couple of seconds but helps your healing - guns do not remove the tissue and just push it to the side which is why most gun piercings have a lumpy bit of tissue next to them, where as needles are hollow and remove the skin for a better healing and feeling piercing."" " What IS a helix piercing for starters? With so many different kinds of ear piercings out there (the days of a singular 'ear piercing' are well and truly gone) - it's easy to feel totally overwhelmed with all the choice. I mean, how are we supposed to know that the words 'helix', 'tragus' and 'daith' are types of piercings and not characters in Harry Potter? If it is a helix piercing that you want, read on to find out exactly wtf it is - aside from being the structure of DNA, obvs - as well as all the variations you can have done and the logistics behind getting your first helix piercing. What is a helix piercing? A helix piercing is any piercing made to the upper cartilage of the ear - but there are different kinds of helix piercings. A standard helix piercing is made in the outer upper cartilage - if you have two or three piercings in the same spot, just above each other, these are called double and triple helix piercings. This is where lobe and cartilage piercings really differ. While you might get over a lobe piercing in around a month, a helix piercing can take anywhere between 3 to 6 months to heal. " The show's viewing numbers have been dropping for the past few years now. The 2018 Victoria's Secret show was watched by fewer people than ever before when it aired on Sunday, 2 December. The catwalk event, which starred the Hadid sisters, as well as Kendall Jenner, attracted a record low of only 3.3 million viewers, compared to five million last year. It was broadcast on ABC in the US and streamed on Hayu for UK viewers. Statista had previously reported that audiences were down by nearly half from 2014 to 2017 from 9.12 million to 4.98 million, a staggering drop. There could be a number of reasons for the decrease. The show is new to ABC, having formerly had a long-standing CBS contract, and it was shown on a Sunday evening rather than its traditional Tuesday slot. Entertainment Weekly reports that ABC also pointed out that the show still secured the best numbers for its 10pm programme all season. Nonetheless, the figures are still an all-time low for the brand, and come as the company faces increasing criticism for its outdated portrayal of beauty and lack of inclusivity. Last month, Victoria's Secret chief marketing officer Ed Razek was forced to apologise for his ""insensitive"" comments made about plus size women and the LGBTQ community. Even Halsey, who performed in the brand's show, publicly shamed the label on Instagram as a result. In June, it emerged that the lingerie giant was struggling to sell even heavily discounted items. Although the study was based on a month’s sales, Jefferies analyst Randal Konik still said that it was ""game over"" for the brand. In an attempt to clear inventory, the label extended the sale by two weeks and dropped prices which resulted in a decrease in margin rates. It’s not the only record of ailing sales. Forbes also reported that comparable store and direct sales of Victoria’s Secret still are 9% below 2016. From: Harper's BAZAAR UK

" In the past few years, the fashion industry has become more size-inclusive… or so it says. Cosmopolitan’s Catriona Innes, a proud size 16, puts that rhetoric to the test. I remember the dress that stole my identity. It was navy blue. It was floral print. Nothing about it stood out in any way. But what it did have – and this is its most important feature – was an elasticated waist. I hated it. I bought it. There was a time when I would have shuddered at the thought of buying such a dress. A plain-girl dress that ensured no one would look when I entered a room. Just a year before, I’d been wearing silk nighties to comedy clubs, cinching in my waist with a beaten-up brown belt that had held up my dad’s flares in the ’70s. My wardrobe had been full of crazily patterned dresses I’d gone at with scissors to ensure they were the perfect length (just above the triangle of freckles high up on my left thigh). Throughout university I would spend hours drawing pictures of future outfits and laying out a riot of different fabrics on my bedroom floor. I knew exactly when Sheffield’s Topshop had new stock, and I’d always be plotting some way to afford it. My size went up and down throughout those years (up during my Strongbow-fuelled first year; down in third year when stress caused my stomach to shoot with pain so badly I couldn’t eat). I never let it affect my style. But what I didn’t realise was that, despite the yo-yoing, I never went above a size 14. And – as I was soon to discover – a size 16 is where an invisible line gets drawn that makes fashion, and shopping, problematic. I first hit that number that year, the “ugly” dress year. I was 24 years old, freshly graduated and suddenly unable to buy the clothes I wanted to match my new London life. It was 2010 and fashion was all about looking wild: smudged eyeliner, skinny legs wrapped up in American Apparel Disco Pants so tight they appeared spray-painted on, topped off with a skull scarf by Alexander McQueen (or whoever was doing a decent enough copy). But the only thing that fit me in American Apparel was a red cotton skirt, elasticated at the waist. I’d go into shops and find that nothing zipped up. And that was when I was on the 14-going-on-16 edge of the sizing scale. Now, eight years on, I’m a 16, often an 18, and my unique, colourful, layered look has all but disappeared. Because the harder shopping and fashion became, the more I removed myself from it. Workwear became the trusty old fit-and-flare, in a stretchy fabric. Clothes stores that were once my staples shut me out. I know which places want me, and which don’t. It’s clear from the sizes on their rails. This – I’m keen to point out – is not just my particular problem, a rant from a woman who can’t accept that she’s put on two stone in two years. ""Clothes stores that were once my staples shut me out"" This is a real problem. Sizes aren’t what they say on the label (H&M recently pledged to alter its own, after a size-12 woman didn’t fit into its 20). Some brands don’t even stock larger sizes (just 13 out of the 25 main high-street stores on London’s busiest shopping location, Oxford Street, stock over a size 16. Eight of them have a plus-size range). And what is on offer is either baggy, dark or hidden away in a special section. There’s even a hashtag: #makemysize – where hundreds of women across the internet post the items they would have bought, if only the bigger size existed. But maybe things have changed. After all, back in 2010, my style icons included Peaches Geldof and Amy Winehouse. In fashion’s eyes, the skinnier the better – no matter how you achieved it. The celebrity closest to my size was Kelly Brook. Now the body-positivity movement has offered me up countless new women to look up to: Felicity Hayward, Tess Holliday, Ashley Graham, Rebel Wilson, Amy Schumer. The average UK woman is a size 16, so the high street could have responded in kind… right? Hitting the street I wrote in my diary, at 15 years old, that when I moved to London I’d shop in the “big Topshop” every day. Now, aged 33, working 10 minutes away, I never go in. It tops my list of “shops where I won’t find anything to fit” despite being spread over three floors. But today I have help. Proper, “cool girl” help in the form of Amy Bannerman, Cosmopolitan’s fashion director. I forgot how brilliant it is in here. I’m wondering why I cut myself off from this shop, as she loads me up with items to go and try on. And then: four items in, I’m reminded. My body, despite my best contortionist efforts, doesn’t fit into the size-16s. I twist, like I’m wringing a dish cloth, to struggle with side zips. I have to lie down, my tummy scooped in, to grapple with metal buttons. My body, despite my best contortionist efforts, doesn’t fit into the size-16s Usually I’d scuttle away with my head down, not looking at the shop assistant as I pass, worrying what she might be thinking. Sometimes I even put the items back myself, so they don’t know I’m too big for their clothes. Amy is more bold. “Do you have any size-18 jeans?” Her words come floating under the door. “Any size-18 jeans?” “Yes, any at all.” There’s a silence. Amy tries again.“How about size-18 dresses?” “That would be rare,” the shop assistant replies. The assistant manages to find me a pair of jeans she thinks will fit: black, skinny with a high waist. And they do up! Yes, they’re digging in so much my stomach has created a shelf, but never mind; I can cover that with a loose top. They fit! I look to see what size they are. The label reads “maternity”. We do manage to leave with a few things: two coats (in sizes smaller than I expected), some jumpers and a dress that didn’t zip up, but that I insisted we took as I loved it so much. Coat, Topshop, £110 Shop now Dress, Monki, £40 Shop now Boots, Office, £85 Shop now Because making things work when they don’t fit is kind of my forte. Too-tight jeans are always worn with long tops. If a dress doesn’t zip up – no problem! That’s easily hidden with a cardigan or suit jacket. I’m used to going into a shop and knowing which items are “safe”: oversized jumpers, stretchy cotton dresses, jeans with elastic in them (I haven’t worn 100% denim in years). But I hadn’t realised how often I settled for items that didn’t work until I forced myself to shop with a professional for a whole day. Usually it’s a quick in-out affair in the changing room, my eyes fixed always on the front mirror (never the back, never the side). If I need something – say for a Christmas party or work event – I’ll take the item that fits, or that I hate the least. It’s amazing what you will put up with just so that you don’t have to go into another changing room and leave feeling defeated. By the time we reach our last shop of the day – River Island – we’re exhausted. We’re told all the plus-size stock from that store has been moved online. “They said there wasn’t demand,” the assistant says, shrugging. The internet appears to be where all the plus-size clothes are hiding: Levi’s goes up to a size 20 online, Oasis’s new plus-size collection is online-only, and even sites like Nasty Gal, Missguided and PrettyLittleThing (places I always assumed were the new American Apparel, AKA not for me) have a range of clothes above a 16. Places like Very and Simply Be are, I’m told, a haven for people who don’t fit into a size-10 mould. Online hauls I have probably ordered clothes online about three times in the past two years. The last time was a sequinned midnight-blue dress from Miss Selfridge that I wanted so badly I ordered it twice (once to be delivered to my London address and once to Edinburgh where the party was going to be). But it was too small and I spent my night tugging it down and wishing that I’d got a bigger size… then remembering that size didn’t exist. I don’t like having to guess what the fabric is like, or how it will fit on my body, from just a cut-out image, or worse, a woman who looks nothing like me. And despite there being more sizes available online, it’s still not great. One brand I note down has 780 dresses in a size 10… but just seven in an 18. A couple only go up to a 14. For the purpose of this feature, we order many, many things. I’m pleasantly surprised. Trends such as layering, that I’d decided were no longer for me, I learn are. Completely see-through dresses become wearable with the right underwear beneath them. And if something doesn’t fit, it doesn’t matter because there’s also the size up, ready and waiting, right there in front of me. Coat, Gap, £50.99 Shop now Dress, Simply Be, £29 Shop now Shoes, Kurt Geiger, £129 Shop now But this isn’t real life. There are 50 items on the rail for me to choose from, which, even on pay day, I couldn’t afford to order. To buy just 10 I’d have to go into my overdraft. Should we really have to go to such great lengths just to find five things that fit? Body lessons Throwing myself back into the high street brought up a jumble of emotions. There was excitement, as I gave away three bags of boring, stretchy dresses. Hope, as I began to plan future looks. Anger, as I realised that, despite a growing body-positive movement, little has actually changed on the shop floor. And pushing itself through the front of all of that was an unexpected twist of guilt, as I realised that by removing myself from fashion, I’d also been removing myself from my body. From how I really felt about it. I’ve done everything I’m supposed to: I’ve found exercise I enjoy, I’ve filled my Instagram feed with body positivity, I chant mantras at myself in changing-room mirrors… But it’s not enough. I still worry that my husband wants me to look a certain way, despite him never expressing it himself. I still feel a failure when I can’t find an outfit for a wedding or Christmas party, even on days when I’ve done well at work or made a friend happy. I even stress that by writing this feature I’m doing something wrong, as I’m not checking my “size privilege” and acknowledging that others can’t find anything on the high street at all. But I don’t want to say “I’m lucky” that after a week of searching, I managed to find some outfits that make me feel like myself. Shouldn’t I, and women like me, be able to impulse-shop in the way others do? I diet, not to fit into a sample size, as many would assume, but to remain within prescribed brackets set for me by the shops I love. I feel my body – one I liken to a lump of playdough that’s not been shaped right – is hard to love quite simply because in most places I’m implicitly being told it’s wrong. Now my new outfits make me feel unstoppable – confident in a way that doesn’t involve a vat of wine and a stern word with myself in the toilet. Fashion, one of the most instant forms of self-expression, shouldn’t leave so many of us feeling unworthy of it.
