But it's not just wheelchair users that accessibility is a struggle for. Columnist Dr Frances Ryan took to Twitter to ask how clothes shopping could be made more accessible for all types of disabilities and her replies were eye-opening. Disabled fashion Twitter! What would make clothes shopping more accessible for you? Are there any shops you particularly love for getting it right? I’m interested in all types of disabilities so please shout. Thx. From problems with changing room sizes and policies... Changing rooms not big enough for Carer to be in there too. Yes! And more awareness among staff: I need my wife to come in with me or else I cannot put the garments on... 🤷‍♀️ Obviously I also need her opinion on what looks good but that’s beside the point 🤫 At least you’re the same gender. Even if the rooms are big enough for 2 most places won’t allow my male partner in with me. I know this but from a male’s prospective, I wish my wife could come in to help me when I try on shorts or pants so that I don’t topple over when putting it on because there are no bars to hold onto in the dressing room. I can’t try trousers/jeans on ANYWHERE! 6 pairs gone back in the last 2 weeks because they don’t fit. Changing Rooms need an additional tier - wheelchair users only, and mobility needs only. Too many using them because they have a pram. I could go on forever. To a lack of detailed descriptions when shopping online. I'm blind and often have trouble buying clothes online. Most shops don't have detailed descriptions available. Usually, the color is the only thing you can find there, sometimes even that's missing. I’m partially sighted. I was just about to say my problem with online shopping is that if there are only one or two choices they often *don’t* describe the colour and I may have to phone (f I can get through) to check if e.g. navy or black. And a lack of seating in-store. places i can sit somewhere if needed, even if just a tiny bench where you try on shoes or something. My issues are not generally severe enough to need a mobility aid, and are far from severe enough to convince the insurance to cover that high cost; Seats in the changing room cubicles, hooks big enough to hang a walking stick off, lifts, enough space between the clothes racks, SEATS EVERYWHERE Lighting can also cause problems. I love shopping but have many stores that I know not to go into because the lighting can trigger partial seizures, (I have epilepsy). I’m sure that I can’t be the only person affected like this and I’m also sure that it wouldn’t take much effort for stores to sort this. Less evil lighting. I can now barely do shops at all as most of the lighting either flickers or is 'glary', often intentionally to ""display the product"". This rapidly makes me ill and I often start falling over within 2 mins of entry to the worst places. I really need to try /1 As well as stores return policies. I think for online shopping, extending the amount of time to do a postal return. Several allow about 2 weeks and if I flare up halfway through I’ve got no chance of talking it myself! People were also quick to Tweet the stores that did cater for disabled people, with Primark, New Look and Marks & Spencer coming out on top. Some of the young wheelchair users we work with were singing Primark's praises - low till counters, larger changing rooms with simple doors I love primark for the fact it has a disabled till point where you can skip the queue and get served quickly. Particularly if I’ve done a lot of walking about and have a basket full haha! New look is great for me, personally. I have constant vertigo so I need to hold onto things and sit down a lot. New look has seats in the changing rooms along with lights I'm not sensitive to. I can't manage much shopping but the little things help my spoons last longer! At my local M&S they have just started trialing this thing where you book an appointment and then they have a special fitter help find the right style of trousers or w.e but the best thing is that the fitter goes and finds the clothes for you! Seeing as so many brands are quick to jump onto the diversity bandwagon, we can only hope that high street shops (and online retailers) actually listen up and implement some of these changes. It's all well and good to have an inclusive advertising campaign, but accessibility for all your customers is the true sign of real inclusivity. Follow Laura on Instagram.

" Fashion blogger Callie Thorpe shares her tips on getting the wardrobe you've always dreamed of. Growing up as an unconfident plus-size teenager, finding clothes was my version of hell. Shopping for fun? Absolutely not. Trying to find clothes on the high street that a, actually fit and b, were fashionable, was impossible. Being plus-size, my options were hugely limited, which only further perpetuated the idea that people above a size 16 weren’t welcome in the fashion world. Fast forward a few years and things have definitely improved for plus-size women. Shopping on the high street is still as difficult as ever however, options for online shopping are now much better and 1,000% more stylish. Part of my job as plus-size style blogger is to share with my readers how I style my outfits, as well as helping them on their journey of self-love and confidence. Being plus-size doesn't mean fashion can't work for you, you've just got to know what to look for. To help you curate the wardrobe you've always dreamed of, I am sharing the tips I've picked up along the way from my years of blogging and personal shopping, because fashion really is for every body. 1. Buy double of things you love When you find something you really love, that fits perfectly, is in your size and makes you feel amazing, buy two of them. It might seem excessive, but sadly when it comes to plus-size fashion, some perfect styles only come around once. So it’s better to be safe than sorry. 2. Shop menswear and maternity You can find some incredibly stylish and unique pieces looking in both these departments. Just because it has a label, doesn’t mean that only those who fit within that label can wear it. My personal favourite place to shop in these sections are ASOS Men Plus and maternity. 3. Don't be afraid to shop in places that don't stock your size Whilst it is frustrating that some stores don’t cater above a size 18, you can sometimes find great options in oversize style pieces. Monki is a great example for this with their Scandinavian style dresses that can fit up to a size 26. 4. Ignore sizing on labels First off, don’t let sizing dictate how you feel about yourself. It’s just a number, it holds no value on you as a person. Sizing differs everywhere, especially when you are plus-size, so don’t be afraid to go up, or even down a size, when finding clothes that you like. As long as it fits and you feel comfortable that’s all that matters. 5. But do make a note of the fit of your favourite brands As mentioned above, sizing online and in-store can differ hugely. A good tip is to keep note of your sizing in your favourite shops. For example, on ASOS, New Look and River Island online sizing is pretty spot on, but with brands like Boohoo, Missguided or Pretty Little Thing, sizing runs small. Being aware of this is so helpful for timesaving, no one wants to spend their life in the post office doing returns. 6. Go get your bra fitted If I could only impart one piece of advice it would be this. Wearing your correct size can change your posture, decrease back pain and make you feel more confident in your clothes. Book yourself in at somewhere like Bravissimo for a fitting and treat yourself to some gorgeous new lingerie. Elomi, Panache and Curvy Kate are three of my favourite full bust lingerie brands to check out. 7. Try everything on When you see something in-store, even if you think it might not work for your body shape, try it. How something looks on a hanger can looks completely different on a body, so give everything a go! 8. Invest in your wardrobe staples One of the best things I own is a woollen black duster coat - it is simple, stylish and chic and it goes with everything. It might cost you more than something you could find from a fast fashion shop, but a timeless piece can see you through every season, regardless of trends. 9. Shop vintage/charity shops I’ll be honest - the plus-size sections of vintage can be sparse; but it's always worth checking them out for any hidden goodies, especially in the men’s section. Look out for cool slogan tees, dungarees, dresses and coats. I once found an old oversize Levi denim jacket for £10 in a shop in Brick Lane. 10. Experiment with colour I used to wear specifically only black clothing, because I thought it would make me look slimmer, but this just simply isn’t true. Colour looks great on all body types. Experiment with what works for you and don’t be afraid to stand out. 11. Ignore plus-size styling rules You can wear stripes, you can wear white, you can wear a crop top. Fashion is about expression not about rules. You deserve to feel good and stylish, so don’t think that you have to hide your body. Confidence comes from within, if you look confident in something that will shine through, so get your arms and legs out in the summer! Follow Callie on Instagram.

" It actually makes a lot of sense. Meghan Markle has impeccable style. She's been a style icon since before she joined the royal family, but ever since her engagement to Prince Harry, she's taken things to the next level. Everything about every look is on-point—that's why some fans have been surprised to notice one fashion quirk of Meghan's: Her shoes are almost always a size or two too big. It's true. Look closely at Meghan's shoes and you'll almost always notice a gap at the heel. Fans especially took note of this with her Royal Ascot outfit. The stunning Givenchy look was paired with black pumps that were noticeably loose. According to fashion expert Harriet Davey, there's a good reason for Meghan's ill-fitting footwear. ""Celebs often go a size up, or even two, in the shoe department when they're at an event or on the red carpet and it's for one reason we can all relate to—to avoid blisters,"" Davey told The Sun. ""There's nothing worse than uncomfortable shoes (we've all been there on a night out) and when celebs like Meghan are wearing heels for a long period of time their feet can often swell up."" This makes sense—especially for someone who spends as much time on her feet (and in heels) as Meghan. ""The swelling can cause blisters and in the long run bunions—like long-time heel fan Victoria Beckham has been rumored to suffer with,"" Davey added. Meghan has been working this fashion trick for a while now—even the shoes she wore at her November 2017 engagement photo call with Harry looked too big. So how does Meghan (and other celebrities who use the same trick) keep her shoes from slipping off when she goes up a size or two? ""A trick of the trade is to stuff the toe with padding like tissue or cotton wool, and this can be taken out once they feel like they need a bit more room in their shoes,"" Davey explained. The more you know. From: Marie Claire US

" They've been a part of her iconic look for more than 70 years. Even when she's not wearing her crown, Queen Elizabeth II always looks regal. The monarch attended the first day of the Royal Ascot on Tuesday in her trademark attire: a bright coat, matching hat, big brooch and, of course, those iconic white gloves. The instantly recognisable wave of her hand lets everyone know Her Majesty has arrived - but that signature greeting wouldn't look quite the same without Cornelia James. The glove manufacturer has supplied the Queen's pairs for more than 70 years. ""The Queen wears gloves because they’ve always been part of her style,"" Genevieve James, creative director of Cornelia James, explained to GoodHousekeeping.com. ""The mind’s eye picture of the Queen is the white gloved hand waving."" Besides the sovereign's innate sense for branding, the signature accessories afford the Queen another benefit. ""They’re number one: style. Number two: practical,"" James adds. ""They’re necessary because if you’re the Queen, you’re shaking a lot of hands, so they protect her hands as well."" The Queen never wears leather or synthetic gloves, preferring a pure cotton with a elegant suede-brushed finish or an even lighter Swiss jersey. The sleeves always end just under her coat, never exposing her arms. The design never strays too far in terms of embellishment or colour either, with the royal preferring simple pairs — appropriately named ""Regina"" on the company's website — in white, black, or parchment, which is a soft ivory. However, the brand first caught the eye of royal couturier Norman Hartnell in 1947 for its use of much brighter hues. Cornelia James, the company founder and Genevieve's mother, fled Austria as a Jewish refugee in 1939. ""She literally arrived in London with just a suitcase full of leather,"" her daughter explains. Her colourful gloves quickly took off in the UK, with the designer receiving placement in Vogue as the ""Colour Queen of England"" not long afterwards. Hartnell, who also designed the Queen's wedding dress, requested a whole suitcase of gloves for Princess Elizabeth's honeymoon as part of her trousseau. Marking the birth of her signature style. Cornelia James received a Royal Warrant in 1979 as the official glove manufacturer to the Queen. Cornelia herself passed away in 1999 at the age of 82, and her daughter has since taken over the family business. James estimates the brand has made approximately 60 to 70 pairs for the Queen since then. The economically-minded customer will wear gloves more than a decade old. ""I can tell the ones I did from the ones my mother did,"" James explains. Given her cost-consciousness, it's no surprise that Cornelia James supplies gloves to more people and businesses than just the Queen. Lady Gaga, Madonna, Taylor Swift, and Rihanna also call themselves customers, not to mention the wardrobe department of Downton Abbey and the stage production of Mamma Mia. The Queen Mother, Princess Margaret and Princess Anne have also worn the brand, but Diana, Princess of Wales, notably set a different fashion precedent when it came to wearing gloves at public engagements. ""She abandoned the royal protocol of wearing gloves because she liked to hold hands when visiting people or shake hands and have direct contact,"" Eleri Lynn, curator of the Kensington Palace exhibit Diana: Her Fashion Story, previously told People. However, the princess did wear wear evening gloves on more than a few formal occasions, ordering her first pair from Cornelia James just a day after encountering the designer. ""My mother once met her at a garden party,"" James recalls. ""She remarked to Princess Diana that she should wear gloves because she noticed the princess bit her finger nails, like I do. She said, 'My daughter bites her nails, you should wear gloves.' The next day we interestingly got a phone call from the palace."" The princess wore their blue gloves with a Bruce Oldfield gown at Claridge's that very night. The Duchess of Cambridge too has donned pairs before, albeit not the white cotton ones. She's frequently worn merino wool gloves from Cornelia James, including on her royal tour to Scandinavia this winter. The royal family's newest fashion icon hasn't tapped the brand yet, but James hopes Meghan will come calling soon as she does more events and shakes more hands. ""I will wait for her to approach us really,"" she said with a laugh. ""I'm sure she will, because she and Prince Harry will be quite active with their duties with the royal family."" Even with a long list of A-list clients, there's still no topping her most loyal customer over the years. ""Working with all these famous faces, the only who's really important to me is the Queen actually,"" James admits. ""They're all important, but the best is the Queen. It doesn't get better than that."" From: Good Housekeeping US

" The best metallic tattoo ideas Metallic tattoos can be super cute, but what if you want something a little more permanent? “I've never seen metallic ink, largely because heavy metals like that are toxic so you're not going to want to put that in your skin. " The move has been applauded by Peta ASOS has announced today that it will no longer sell silk, cashmere, mohair or feathers on its platform. The decision – which has been made on the basis of preventing cruelty to animals – has been praised by Peta. ""Peta applauds ASOS for leading the charge for compassion in fashion,"" Peta's director of corporate projects, Yvonne Taylor said. ""In response to Peta's campaigns, consumers are changing the face of the industry by demanding that designers and retailers ditch animal-derived materials in favour of cruelty-free alternatives that look great without causing suffering."" ASOS is not the first retailer to ban the sale of mohair. Topshop, Marks & Spencer and H&M have all pledged to stop using the material after Peta exposed the mohair industry for the cruel techniques used. However, ASOS has gone one step further by banning the use of a number of other materials, many of which consumers may not have ever considered to be in this category of cruelty. The production of silk, for example, kills 6,600 silkworms (through boiling or gassing them alive whilst in their cocoons) just to make one kilogram of silk. Cashmere goats are frequently shorn in midwinter despite needing their coats to protect them from the cold, meaning that many die as a result of this exposure, whilst young goats with defects are slaughtered. ASOS has promised that by January 2019, nothing it sells will include any of these cruelly obtained materials. From: Harper's BAZAAR UK

" Because peeing in a big gown is not easy Wearing a big, beautiful wedding dress is all well and good - but what happens when you stop just posing for pictures and actually need to go to the toilet? Trying to get up underneath all those layers could steal precious dancing time away from you, or end in accidents! Thankfully, one woman is here to save future brides from wedding day toilet-related disasters. Panicking before her wedding that she'd struggle to be able to go to the toilet in her mermaid wedding dress, this bride took a pair of scissors to an Ikea bag and created a new accessory for the day. She wrote on Facebook: ""Well, I got married a few weeks ago (in a mermaid wedding dress) and I was really worried about going to the bathroom and not being able to … handle myself. Someone helping or watching me going to the bathroom on my wedding day? Not being able to have free hands to use the toilet paper? Or even worse if my period decides to show? NO WAY! ""My bridal bathroom helper hack costs about 0.80 euro and I did it the day before my wedding. It took only 3 minutes. What I like best is it’s almost free and allows me to make my life easier on my wedding day. So here is the hack."" Basically, cut a whole in the bottom of an Ikea bag, then pull up the bag catching all your dress as you go. Hook your arms through the straps and voila! You can wee in peace! The internet being the internet did have a few questions such as: WHY IS SHE WEARING BLACK PANTS ON HER WEDDING DAY THOUGH?! But it also led to a load of other brides sharing their tips for peeing happily in a wedding dress. One wrote: ""I just took mine off in the hotel room before going the toilet. I don't really drink so I only had to go a few times throughout the day"". Another suggested: ""I've been advised that it is easier when wearing a wedding dress to use the loo facing backwards! May need someone to hold up the skirt but possibly a little more private."" And another shared: ""My dress was huge with a very long train. I was commando for the reception and I lifted the front of my dress and sat on it front ways if that makes sense. I didn't have any help once to go to the loo."" Or if none of that sounds good you could try buying this clever Bridal Buddy gizmo(£39.99).

" And discovered the best ones for a bum lift. I am in Selfridges’ changing rooms struggling to hoist a pair of skinny jeans up over my belly. I’ve worn granny pants instead of a thong, and now realise the gravity of this mistake. I turn around and catch sight of my arse in the mirror. Even Selfridges’ lighting can’t disguise the fact it now looks like four Dairylea Triangles. I feel teary. When did this happen? When did my backside decide to look more like my mum’s? And can a pair of ‘miracle’ jeans really help me get my own bum back? To answer that, I need to go on a journey. A long journey. A journey that will involve lots of denim. Lots of looking at my arse. And lots of existential questioning conducted in high-street fitting rooms across the world. When I was a teenager, I loved my bum. I mean really loved it. It was cute and round like a Granny Smith apple, and slipped into my low-rise Hollister jeans as easily as a reality star slides into a protein-shake endorsement. ""My teenage bum is long gone"" Of course, back in my day, boobs, rather than arses, were the thing, so I didn’t really give much thought to what was going on behind me. But, oh my, how things have changed. I’m 27 now, and a new derrière fixation has swept the globe (thanks, Kim K) – at the exact moment I fell out of love with my own arse. I’m not completely down on myself – I have the same insecurities as every girl. I’ve just got to come to terms with the fact that my teenage bum is long gone. My Instagram feed is flooded with Lycra-encased booties as round and delicious as bagels, while arse-plumping injectables – and their bountiful results – can be seen bouncing up and down streets across the globe. So I joined a gym, and subjected myself to all sorts of weird-sounding moves and apparatus that claimed to hoist my bum back to its rightful place. The results are thus far proving elusive. But then, one day, it occurs to me. I work in fashion – an entire industry devoted to the art of visual manipulation. What if, while I wait for the gym to pay off, I could find a pair of jeans that did the hard work for me? After all, the denim world has come a long way since my boot-cut ’90s-jeans wardrobe. There are now jeans that can do pretty much everything bar give you liposuction when you zip them up. With this in mind, I began my search for the perfect arse-sculpting pair. And that search, like most things in my life, starts with Instagram. I post a poll on my feed, asking friends what their favourite jeans are. A few mention Gap, which I haven’t actually considered since about 1995. I ‘pop’ in, and among the piles of sweatshirts, tees and veritable jumble sale of other items, I find a lovely, calm corner of denim. Two hours later, I’m still in there. I pull on an intriguingly titled pair called Mid-Rise Curvy True Skinny and notice my bum looks rounder and juicier than usual. Buy now Gap Mid Rise Curvy True Skinny Jeans, £54.95 My next stop is a brand called Mother, whose name I have heard referenced in exalted tones on Instagram. I try the Shift Insider Ankle, whose extended high waist looks cool on the website model – not so much on me. My bum looks about two miles long. The Looker Ankle, with a slightly lower waist, suits me much better. A brand that I’ve been fan-girling over for some time, Stoned Immaculate, does some crazy ’70s flares with a huge star on the bum. They look incredible on the bloggers that post hazy, artistic #OOTDs in them, but definitely do not have the same effect on me. The star’s points are angled downward, which somehow makes my bum look depressed, and the seams pinch inwards at the wrong places. ""Turns out skin-tight jeggings are not my thing"" Re/Done – an interesting brand that takes vintage Levi’s and re-sews them into modern cuts, as well as producing their own styles – fares better, though the price (around £200) is slightly eye-watering. They are my fashion director’s favourite, and I have my heart set on the High Rise Crop Flare and the Crawford, but neither work. I’m gutted, because they look incredible on their more famous fans – so why not me? Instagram sends me to all corners of the denim universe, introducing me to brands I’d never tried, including Kings Of Indigo (cool, but not enough support in the arse area) and Freddy (turns out skin-tight jeggings are not my thing). After exhausting Instagram, I turn to celebrities with famous behinds (though I assume personal-training sessions have much to do with that). The Kardashians are arguably the most famous walking-talking rears in the world, and Khloé even has her own line of jeans, Good American. I try the Good Cuts and Good Legs styles (they’re classics, apparently), but they just don’t sit right on me. The pairs that fit my bum gape at the waist, and vice versa. They’re very comfortable, and look banging on the Kardashian-Jenners, but don’t suit my body shape. Frame is a brand loved by the celebrity set – the Hadids, Taylor Swift and Miranda Kerr are all fans, though I suspect winning the genetic lottery also plays a part. The Frame PR kindly sends me their Le High Skinny style to trial, and they’re so comfortable and stretchy I even wear them on my eight-hour flight home to America for a family holiday.On US soil, I run into an ex-boyfriend. I ask him what he thinks of my jeans. Without further prompting, he says my “ass looks good” in them. They’re a little pricey at £203, but they’re so comfy that their cost-per-wear ratio is probably worth it. (Frame’s Le Original pair, however, makes me look wider than normal due to the wide-set pockets.) While in the land of denim (Americans, as with most things, like to say they invented jeans – although Levi Strauss was actually a German immigrant), I try a US brand called DL1961. They claim to have 98% ‘shape retention’. I opt for the Florence Crop Mid Rise Skinny jeans and, lo and behold, my arse looks as neat and round as a dim sum. The problem: as with most of the best jeans I find, they’re not cheap – £140 – so I’d only be able to justify a couple of pairs per year – and that’s if I lived off party canapés. Time to call in the experts. I get in touch with Kelly Harrington, the print designer and trend forecaster at H&M, whose Instagram account (@kellouhar) is a denim addict’s secret fix. I tell her what I’m looking for, and she says the most flattering jeans on the rear should always have a high, upward-angled ‘V’ yoke (that’s the seam that runs above the back pocket but under the waist), as that helps lift the eye upwards, creating an anti-gravity effect. She also says smaller, higher pockets draw the eye upwards and inwards, creating that lifted, peachy look. Finally, she tells me that stretch jeans with around 2-5% elastane keep their shape well, but 100% cotton jeans (AKA zero stretch) are stiffer, and therefore hold you in. ""The higher pockets really do make a difference"" I search for pairs with higher pockets. The J Brand Mid-Rise Capri sits about two inches higher than the line where my bum meets the top of my leg, and Kelly was right: RESULT! It looks lifted and sexy. In fact, these are seriously hot jeans, definitely first-date-worthy… maybe I’ll re-download Tinder? Focus, Maddy. Focus... The Paige Hoxton Ankle Peg High Rise Skinny have the same effect – the higher pockets and angled yoke really do make a difference. I feel like I’m starting to get this down to a science. H&M has a style called the Shaping Skinny, which has the high yoke and a smidgen of stretch. And yes… score! Armed with this new information, it’s incredible how easy it is to find a pair that works. I give you, in no order of preference: AllSaints Grace; Levi’s Altered Wide Leg (which lifts and makes your waist look teeny); and pretty much every pair from Wrangler’s Body Bespoke range all have those key lifted pockets – I can see myself wearing its Cropped Flare Dancing Days with espadrilles all summer, and the Slim Body Bespoke is a fantastically flattering skinny. A friend suggests that the Citizens Of Humanity Liya is a good stiff jean, and I really love it. It’s an amazing slim leg that feels like it holds in my stomach and bum due to the stiffer cotton (which somehow still feels soft). Tick, tick, and tick. At £335, though, I’d need to Ebay half my stuff to afford a pair. By the day of my photoshoot, I had tried on 132 pairs of jeans. I now have an arsenal of arse-helpers to wear from work to late-night bar, with my absolute all-round favourite (for value, fit and comfort) being the Gap Mid-Rise Curvy True Skinny. But I also know this: denim is a science. Don’t be swayed by the very clever marketing names every pair now comes with – you need knowledge. Take at least five pairs of jeans into a fitting room with you and choose one size above and below what you think you are – they will all look different. And pay just as much attention to the pockets as you do the leg shape. Why we’ve never been told this, I do not know. But most of all what I have learned is this: when you take your jeans off at the end of the night, you’re still going to have the arse that life has decided to give you. The right pair of jeans can just help you love it a little bit more. The Technical bit - Crack the yoke code The yoke is the seam that’s below the waistband but above the pocket. How curved or angled it is has a huge effect on your rear view.The Inverted Arc - Gives the illusion of fuller, more rounded buttocks. A Horizontal Yoke - line will make your waist look wider.“V” Shape - The most popular and flattering cut for all figures.Sweetheart - Creates instant ice-cream-scoop curves. Tasty.Extra Wide - Ideal for the teen ‘falling pants’ look – but little else. Maddy's dressing room guide DON’T wear granny pants (*sob*)DO wear a seamless thong - This ensures your jeans fit smoothly with no added lumps and bumps. Briefs can pinch inwards and create a distorted silhouette.DON’T shop while you’re PMS-ing DO wait until your cycle has finished - Period bloat can force you to go up two to three sizes, and you’ll end up with a baggy fit.DON’T dress for the ArcticDO wear layers - This way, you can strip down when you work up a sweat. Slip-on shoes are good for making multiple trips back and forth, too. A tight tee or vest will let you easily check out the shape of the jean.DON’T go it aloneDO Use the personal shopping services - These are offered free by some of the bigger stores. Call ahead, tell them your size and have a selection waiting for you, instead of trawling around the shop floor. Follow Maddy on Instagram.

" Lauren Nicole suffered from body dysmorphia before she was scouted online. As a size 18/20 plus-size blogger, 20-year-old Lauren Nicole suffered from body dysmorphia, but after being scouted on Instagram she quickly found herself modelling for the very first time in nothing but her swimwear. While this might seem daunting for anyone, Lauren explains how modelling actually helped her to finally accept her own body. Running her own fashion blog, The Fashion Killer, Lauren was used to taking pictures of herself, but she had never done any professional modelling until a plus-size fashion company slid into her DMs. ""I started posting more personal style images on my blog in 2016 and then an independent plus size brand, 113, found my Instagram and said they would love to work with me. At that point I just thought it was on a blogger level, but they asked if I would like to become a brand ambassador and within that came modelling."" Oh hi 20! Thank you for all the birthday wishes yesterday, I had a fab day. Bring on the weekend😜 A post shared by Lauren-Nicole (@laurennicolefk) on Dec 13, 2017 at 8:39am PST Despite having never modelled before, Lauren was quite literally thrown in at the deep end. ""They had a shoot coming up the next week and asked me to model their debut swimwear collection - I had never done any modelling before! I was just so excited that they were interested in me and when they said I'd be shooting with Felicity Hayward I knew I had to say yes."" ""When I saw the pictures I had a breakdown"" It was over four months after the shoot took place that Lauren finally saw the pictures for the first time. ""I remember so clearly it was a Wednesday, I was at school and they sent me the images and when I saw them I had a breakdown. I couldn't believe what I'd signed myself up for - I wasn’t the most body confident and I'd never done anything like that before."" ""I didn't really go into it thinking about the pictures that would come out at the end. And at the time, I really didn't like any of the final images, I was just very much in my own head. Now though, I look back at them and do like them all."" After her shoot came out, Lauren was approached by a scout from IMM Models who asked her to come into their offices for measuring. ""They were very thorough, they measured my thighs, my arms, length of my arms, width of my arms, pretty much everything except for my ankles. I'm quite short for a model at 5'7, so I really didn't think I'd get signed."" ""I definitely felt like I wasn't big enough"" In the UK plus-size modelling starts at a size 12 but as Lauren explains there is a lot of pressure to fit a certain standard. ""Sometimes you’ll see 'curve models' and they’re a size 12/14 and then sometimes you’ll see others like Chanelle Mustafa who are a size 22. When I started I was a size 16/18 and although no one from the plus-size community said it, at times I felt that I wasn’t big enough because I was on the slightly smaller end of the scale. It's strange because now I’m a size 18/20, I sometimes feel too big."" me doing anything at all: omg I’m such wifey material😂... A post shared by Lauren-Nicole (@laurennicolefk) on Feb 5, 2018 at 11:42am PST As Lauren puts it, ""I think it's important that women feel represented. I can imagine if I were a size 26/28, it would be frustrating to see a size 16/18 person modelling clothes for my size, because I wouldn't be able to picture what those clothes would actually look like on me. It's as though there is still this kind of beauty standard of what 'acceptable' plus-size is."" Although you might think having a fashion blog and posting lingerie pictures on Instagram can only be done by someone with the kind of confidence to rival Elle Woods, Lauren hasn't always been so secure about her own body. ""It’s so strange because prior to modelling I was very insecure about my body. I suffered from body dysmorphia and I didn’t treat my body the way that I should have."" ""Growing up there were no plus-size models who were considered sexy or beautiful"" While she may have initially hated those very first swimwear shots, modelling has actually been the one thing that's given Lauren the confidence she needed. ""Not only has modelling given me confidence, but seeing other women who have bodies like mine has really helped me. When I was growing up there were no plus-size models who were considered sexy or beautiful, especially within the black community. She was either the mother or the aunt, or the funny girl. If attending university and modelling in her spare time isn't enough, Lauren still keeps her fashion blog running. ""Being able to straddle the blogger/model side really works for me as I actually get a lot of job opportunities through my social media. " According to how often you wear everything When you buy a new item of clothing, what do you weigh up in your head? Perhaps how good it looks on you, how many occasions you'll be able to wear it, what it will go with from your existing wardrobe etc etc. But do you stop to consider the cost per wear? You see, there are some items that we wear so much, they actually become cheaper because of all the use we are getting out of them. Consider a dress that you buy for a wedding and you wear twice, it cost £100 but really you've spent £50 per use. Compare that to your fave pair of £40 Topshop jeans that you wear every weekend without fail, and you're looking at a much cheaper cost per wear. And now someone has done the actual maths to work out what the cheapest items in our wardrobes are - according to how often we wear them. My Voucher Codes surveyed 2,586 people from around the UK on their shopping habits - including how much they tend to spend on certain items and how often they wear particular clothes. What they found is that we actually tend to spend more on those items that we wear less, and rarely splash out on the clothes that we use a lot. Dresses, for example, had an average of just three wears, despite an average spend of £40 while pyjamas were worn 40 times on average and cost just £14. Here's the full run-down of Voucher Codes' findings: Garment type Av. Spend Av. Wears Cost Per Wear Dresses £40 3 £13.33 Lingerie £27 5 £5.40 High heels £19 8 £2.38 Trousers £38 19 £2.00 Swimwear £22 12 £1.83 Activewear £58 34 £1.71 Coats/jackets £75 54 £1.39 Workwear £62 65 95p Shoes £28 35 80p Skirts £26 38 68p Jumpers £31 54 57p Shorts £21 46 46p Trainers £42 91 46p Nightwear £14 40 35p T shirts £17 95 18p Underwear £4.50 36 13p Jeans £28 298 9p Louisa Marsden, fashion spokesperson at My Voucher Codes, said: “Many of us base our purchasing decisions on the price of items, but there’s an argument that we should be considering an item’s value in the longer term. It’s clear to see we spend more on items we wear a couple of times, like dresses and fancy lingerie, compared to basics like t-shirts and jeans, which are a go-to for everyday wear. So, even if it feels like a blow to your wallet to start with, it’s definitely worth spending more on certain clothing if it means you’ll get more bang for your buck!""

" The high street brand is cutting prices in a bid to turnaround the business New Look is closing 60 stores around the UK, due to financial troubles and tough tradition conditions. While this is bad news for the high street retailer, the chain has announced details of its turnaround plan and there's some great news for fans of the brand. New Look is lowering its pricing across its clothing range, with 80% of its product retailing for under £20. The company said the move marks its ""return to value-led fast fashion"" in a bid to boost sales. The latest financial report revealed that like for like sales have dropped more than 11 per cent over the last year in stores and 19 per cent online. The decision to cut prices comes after New Look sought a Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA) in March in an attempt to reduce costs. The brand has proposed to ""deliver financial and operational stability"" in the months to come. ""Since November, we have focused on making the necessary changes to get the company back on track and reconnect with our customers,"" Alistair McGeorge, Executive Chairman, said in a statement. ""Our turnaround plan is now well underway, and we have already made substantial operational improvements to help stabilise the business, reduce our fixed cost base and put us in a better position to drive future full price sales."" New Look is the latest retailer to feel the pressure of falling profits in recent months. Both Toys R Us and Maplin went into administration in February. Earlier this month, House of Fraser announced plans to close 31 of its 59 shops, including its London Oxford Street flagship, as part of a restructuring strategy.

" The Princess of Wales didn't just repeat outfits - she remade them completely. The Duchess of Cambridge may re-wear key pieces from her wardrobe from time to time, but her late mother-in-law Princess Diana completely deconstructed and redesigned several outfits to suit her changing style. Below, a few of the princess's best ""recycled"" looks. Diana wore this long-sleeved gown for the first time during an official visit to Lisbon, Portugal in 1987. She then remade the dress, removing the sleeves and re-crafting it with a heart-shaped strapless neckline to wear to a charity ball two years later in 1989. Clearly, Diana brought a few of her favourite looks with her to Lisbon in 1987. The photo on the left shows her on the official visit, and in the picture on the right, she's in Cannes just a few months later, wearing the same skirt, just styled a bit differently. Diana was even inventive with her jewellery. In May of 1986, she wore a headband made from jewels, which she had reset from the Saudi suite of sapphires. The gems reportedly came from a watch, and she wore the new look both around the head and as a choker necklace. Diana was a big fan of polka dots. On the left, she's seen with Princess Anne at an equestrian event in June of 1986, and on the right, she appears to be wearing an altered version of the same dress, sans-peplum, at a polo match just one year later. Diana wasn't afraid to break apart a two-piece set to make multiple outfits. On the left, she's seen in the full ensemble at the 1981 Wimbledon Tennis Championships. Several years later, in 1985, she wore just the skirt to a polo match in Cirencester. Two years after Princess Diana wore a striking floral gown to meet the president of Nigeria, she wore the same top with a different skirt to a banquet in Seoul, South Korea. Sapphires were one of Diana's signature stones. On the left, the late Princess of Wales wore her striking sapphire brooch as a pin while at the Dutch royal family banquet at Hampton Court Palace in 1982. On the right is a portrait of Diana wearing the same brooch set into a pearl necklace in Vienna in 1986. On the left, Diana wears a Mondi white skirt with red polka dots with matching ankle socks at a polo match in Windsor in June, 1986. And on the right, she receives flowers from well-wishers during a visit in Melbourne, Australia in the same skirt! Members of the royal family are quite fond of their plaid, and Diana was no exception. The late princess favoured this tartan suit by Caroline Charles. She wore it to the Braemar Highland Games in Scotland in 1981 and then changed up the neckline before she wore it again in 1985. Diana wore this notable pastel evening gown twice, once in Melbourne in 1983 (left) and again without the peplum and with shorter sleeves (right) in 1986. " One of the first memories I have related to fashion was being a kid and buying a pair of shoes that were entirely covered in rainbow glitter. They were as fantastic as you might imagine. I remember my mother turning to the sales lady and saying, “don’t we all wish we could have a pair of those?” And thinking to myself, “wait, why can’t you?” That was before Kate Spade. Kate Spade changed so much when she started her line in 1993. That was a time when cool adult fashion consisted of overalls and plaid shirts. And into that grungy world, Kate Spade entered with preppy bags in a variety of wildly bright colours. ""Kate Spade seemed to understand that women who liked wearing pink dresses weren’t stupid or frivolous."" The line spoke to women who still wanted to be girly, who never saw anything wrong with being girly. Not everyone wanted to emulate the actors from The Craft (though, to be fair, the women on the Craft poster looked great). And, inspired by vintage handbags, Kate Spade allowed them to embrace that feminine spirit. Time Magazine wrote about how she “persuaded women in the '90s to trade what she calls 'the nothing black bag' for a purse with personality.” I suspect not all that much persuasion was necessary. Women were just waiting for an affordable option that allowed them to have a little fun with fashion. And, God, her pieces had personality. Inspired by her mother’s old handbags that came in a variety, “oranges, pinks, chocolates, huge pearl buttons,” Kate Spade’s bags were never nothing black bags. Go to the company’s website today and you’ll see that her first collection inspired a range of bags that look like pineapples, purses covered in comic print, totes that declare they’re “out and about” and clutches emblazoned with flamingos. In 2003, The New York Times wrote that, “If Dorothy Parker were a product, she would be a Kate Spade clutch.” That may account for the dizzying number of Kate Spade products with Dorothy Parker quotes emblazoned upon them. Like Dorothy Parker, Kate Spade’s pieces started conversations. And it wasn’t just the handbags. The whole line seemed able to find the fun in femininity without ever making fun of femininity. Kate Spade seemed to understand that women who liked wearing pink dresses weren’t stupid or frivolous because of that style choice—after all, she proudly donned pink tights and founded a multimillion dollar empire. It was an affordably priced wardrobe made for the Elle Woods of the world. And if you’re looking for a pair of sparkle shoes, your first stop should be Kate Spade. They’ve made countless glittery pairs of shoes since they started doing footwear in 1999. My mother and I both have pairs of her shoes now. Today, Mindy Kaling tweeted that Spade’s clothes “were colourful, bold, cheerful, and encouraged women to find the twinkly person inside them. You couldn’t walk into her boutiques and not smile.” I am heartbroken about the news of Kate Spade. I have worn her clothes many, many times. They were colorful, bold, cheerful, and encouraged women to find the twinkly person inside them. You couldn’t walk into her boutiques and not smile. Rest In Peace, Kate. Kate Spade taught us that we can still enjoy colour and sparkle, and that fashion can be as playful as it was when we were children. We can still be twinkly in adulthood. It was fashion that focused on making people happy. Which is one of the reasons why it’s so tragic that Kate Spade's life ended with such sadness. It seems shocking, always, when someone who has brought so much joy into the lives of so many takes their own life, as Kate Spade did. The fact that many of us will miss her creative gifts certainly has nothing on the pain that her family must be feeling. But will miss those gifts, all the same. She was inspiring to many of us. The world will be a less sparkling place for the loss of her. But the twinkly person she inspired in many of us will hopefully go on, in shoes that she created for us. If you or someone you know is exhibiting warning signs of suicide, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 800-273-TALK (8255). From: Harper's BAZAAR US

" The Duchess of Cambridge rarely strays from it There's one thing you may never have noticed about the Duchess of Cambridge's footwear choices: she always wears closed-toe shoes. For official engagements or outings where she's representing the royal family, Kate will opt for a pair of neat court shoes - which may vary in colour or texture, but consistently give her outfit a formal finishing touch. Turns out that it's not just a personal preference; it's etiquette. ""Open-toed shoes are considered informal footwear,"" etiquette expert William Hanson told Harper's Bazaar UK, ""and inappropriate for formal occasions"". Female guests at the royal wedding were instructed to avoid open-toe shoes. It was requested that they also opt for dresses that covered their shoulders and fell below the knee. Tights, too, were encouraged. ""Regardless of how relatively relaxed it was in the grande scheme and precedent of the British monarchy, May’s royal wedding was still a formal affair and so it was quite right that guests were asked to avoid wearing open-toed shoes,"" Hanson said, before calling out several high-profile guests for going against the dress code, blaming their ""egos"". ""Sadly the celebrity-heavy guest list was evident quite quickly, especially in the foot department, as some of the guests’ egos took over and pushed protocol to the back seat, namely Priyanka Chopra, Troian Bellisario and Chelsey Davy,"" he said. ""It is a shame many decided they were above the dress code: if you do not like the dress code at an event, don’t go."" When Meghan stepped out at her first post-wedding event last week - a party to celebrate Prince Charles' 70th birthday at Buckingham Palace - much was made of her decision to wear nude tights, something which is also encouraged of royal females and considered 'proper' etiquette. This could also go some way as to explain the penchant for a closed-toe shoe; no one wants to see unsightly seam-covered toes. “Tights are also required for formal day and evening wear, and while not explicitly linked to the shoe choice they are certainly a natural accompaniment,"" explained Hanson. ""Ladies (and gentlemen) being modestly covered is perhaps a hang over from the Victorian era, who did tend to be a tad prudish at times.” While their outfits are often more relaxed, Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie will also most often be seen in a closed-toe shoe, as will Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall, and, of course, the Queen. The number of times the Duchess of Cambridge has publicly worn peep-toes or sandals can be counted on one hand; she's fond of a strappier heel under a full-length dress (perhaps because, for once, nude tights aren't required), but this tends to be at glitzier film premieres or Hollywood events. She also opted for a pair of sandals for a trip to the beach in Australia - which undoubtedly even the Queen would be accepting of. So it looks as though the new Duchess of Sussex will be incorporating an array of multi-coloured court shoes into her wardrobe for the forseeable future, but we're looking forward to seeing her interpretation of the royal dress code. " Squad goals Your summer holiday with the squad is fast approaching. Cut to montage in your head of you and your besties in all your holiday outfits - on the beach, in the club, by the pool. But, to live out those summer fashion dreams IRL and avoid an excess baggage meltdown half an hour in, you need to nail your holiday packing. The easiest way to stem the tide of playsuits and sliders? Plan out your outfits for each day in advance - snap them on your phone and resist the urge to throw anything else in the case (you really don't need that last minute kaftan). Cut to you looking smug at check-in. Hand luggage only = holiday goals. Set the tone right from take-off with a well-thought-out travel outfit. Ditch the skinny jeans because, y’know, circulation, and swap in some cropped wide-leg trousers instead. Then, add some stripes (classic holiday vibes) with a cute T-shirt or oversized shirt. Layer up as much as possible: A vest top under a shirt, a thin knit over a T-shirt and a denim jacket on top. They can all be worn later on in the holiday and those extra layers mean more space in your suitcase. Win-win. An outfit that can take you from sightseeing to seeing the sun come up is what the capsule holiday wardrobe is all about. We love printed tailored shorts that can be worn with a casual shirt and sandals during the day and then dressed up with a cami, some statement jewellery and heels for evening. Pro tip: Always pack one casual and one smart top for every bottom. When you're serving Miami beach realness, you need colour, bold prints and co-ords. Swimsuits and bikinis are what you’ll be wearing for 75% of your hols and they take up the least amount of space, so it’s perfectly acceptable to take three minimum for a five-day break. Then, you need a couple of T-shirts, a cute playsuit and that perfect pair of denim cut-offs for hanging by the pool in style. *orders another piña colada* This is ‘jeans-and-a-nice top’ vacay-style. Upgrade your usual night-out look and bring the holiday vibes with tops that show off those sun-kissed shoulders – wear them with high waisted jeans so you can still rinse the breakfast buffet in the morning. Then go extra with your accessories – tassel earrings and serious heels are the one. For all your summer wardrobe goals, check out V by Very

" Her second outfit included a ""something blue."" Meghan Markle a.k.a. the brand-new Duchess of Sussex stunned everyone in not one but two stunning wedding dresses this weekend at her nuptials to Prince Harry. Clare Waight Keller, Artistic Director at Givenchy, designed the first look worn at the ceremony in St. George's Chapel and subsequent reception in St. George's Hall. The simple yet stunning ensemble of course wowed the groom — ""She just looked absolutely exquisite,"" he told Waight Keller afterwards — but admittedly underwhelmed some viewers looking for more sparkle and a tighter fit. A second glamorous look by Stella McCartney fit right in with the vibes of the second reception at Frogmore House. (Prince Harry himself changed into a snappy tux!) While it's nearly impossible to pick a favourite, here's what even the most devoted royal fans may have missed about these gorgeous gowns during all of the hubbub of the big day. Markle surprised everyone by picking the historic French fashion house for her wedding gown instead of a British label, but the choice clearly reflected her own simple yet chic style. ""The dress epitomises a timeless minimal elegance referencing the codes of the iconic House of Givenchy and showcasing the expert craftsmanship of its world-renowned Parisian couture atelier,"" the palace revealed in a statement. Not only was the late actress a muse for Givenchy, but she often wore similar cuts. The shoulder-framing bateau neckline and sculpted waist seen on Markle's dress could have easily appeared on the movie star decades ago. The wedding dresses of Queen Elizabeth II, Diana, Princess of Wales, and the Duchess of Cambridge all featured elaborate beading, lace, and other details. Given its simplicity, Markle's likely cost less than the £250,000 price tag for Kate Middleton's, but still likely fell in the six-figure range. Waight Keller and Markle picked a pure white double bonded silk cady to bring a ""fresh modernity"" to her look instead. ""Perfect for the round sculptural look required, the silk cady has a soft matt lustre,"" the palace revealed. While the dress remained plain, the 16-foot-long veil did not. Markle requested that her wedding look represent all 53 Commonwealth countries, and the elaborate embroidery on her headpiece did the trick. Following significant research, the design team picked a distinctive flower for each nation. Then the textile artists spent hundreds of hours meticulously sewing them in three dimensions onto the tulle. The frequent handwashing kept the threads pristine and perfectly white. Besides the honouring the Commonwealth, Markle included several other important symbols as well. A California poppy pays homage to her birthplace. Wintersweet, a type of shrub, grows in front of the couple's cottage at Kensington Palace. Finally, the design incorporated crops of wheat interspersed among the flowers to symbolise love and charity. With all that veil it's easy to miss how long the dress actually stretched. The hem itself doesn't look too far off Kate Middleton's 9-foot-long train, but of course both measure far short of Princess Diana's 25-foot behemoth. The couture helm used silk duchess satin instead of the dress's silk cady. This fabric holds its shape well because of its high thread count; it's actually the most common material used for bridal gowns, royal or not. Queen Mary's diamond bandeau features a detachable brooch of 10 brilliant diamonds in the centre, which King George V's wife sometimes swapped out for other gems. The circa-1893 pin Markle wore actually only became an element of the tiara with the creation of the frame in 1932. The 11 sections of the pavé set band feature interlaced ovals, an Art Deco motif more in tune with Markle's personal style than some of the other floral options floated about. The piece hadn't appeared in public for decades, but Markle had worn her Cartier earrings at least three times before the wedding, meaning she'll probably bring them out again in the future. Markle turned to one of her favourite brands for the nude mesh stilettos she wore with her Stella McCartney dress to the second reception. They had a sweet detail hidden inside; the soles were painted a baby blue. The bride wore another pair of Cartier earrings (they appear to match the bracelet she had on in the morning!) but she also added a little extra sparkle on her right hand. The emerald-cut aquamarine gem once belonged to her late mother-in-law. What a sweet way to honour her on the couple's wedding day! From: Good Housekeeping US

" It's on loan from The Queen! Congratulations are in order for Prince Harry and Meghan Markle who are now officially husband and wife! As for details, the new Duchess of Sussex wore her hair tied back in a low-bridal bun and the veil was fixed on with a diamond bandeau tiara. The tiara was lent to the bride by the Queen and previously belonged to her grandmother Queen Mary. Queen Mary was gifted the brooch - which is in the centre part of the tiara and features a whopping ten diamonds - in 1893 on her marriage to Prince George, Duke of York who later became King George V. Years later, in 1932, the diamond and platinum bandeau was specifically made in order to accommodate the brooch. The bandeau has eleven sections, featuring interlaced ovals and pavé along with large and small brilliant diamonds. Queen Mary officially bequeathed the tiara to Queen Elizabeth II in 1953. Other pieces of Markle’s jewellery, including the earrings and bracelet, were made by the designers Cartier. From: Good Housekeeping UK

Buy now Curves Green Stripe Wide Leg Trousers, Newlook.com, £22.99 Buy now Green Stripe Wide Leg Trousers, Newlook.com, £19.99 Before anyone even tries to come at me with the argument that this is down to the use of more fabric, why are the exact same trousers in the petite range the same price as the main range? " Clothes hangers are like magnets to wheelchairs. Shopping on the high street when you're in a wheelchair is rarely a bundle of laughs. There are several challenges we encounter every time we want a bit of retail therapy, and as a fashion vlogger, I experience these struggles a lot: 1. I'm in a wheelchair, so I need to use a lift to get to another floor. But in most high street shops, especially on a weekend, there’s usually a queue for the lift. Of course this mainly consists of wheelchair-users and people with buggies, but there are always a couple of lurkers at the front of the queue who are fully capable of taking the stairs. I normally just stare at them hoping they’ll get the message and move on, though my tactic doesn’t always work. 2. Over the festive season I decided to go shopping on Black Friday. Yes, I know it was probably a crazy decision, but I spotted a shop that was offering up to 75% off and I wasn't going to miss that kind of bargain. I saw a long waistcoat sitting among various other things, but struggled to reach it so asked my PA if she could grab it for me. As I finished my sentence, another girl pushed in front of me and grabbed it off the rails; I was in such shock that I didn’t know what to do. I followed her around the shop hoping she would put it down, but no such luck. Should have stuck to Cyber Monday. Oh shit. Did I miss Coachella? 🎡 . . . . . . . #coachella #festivalvibes #pink #glitter #festival #fashionvlogger #beautyvlogger A post shared by Shelby (@shelbykinsxo) on Apr 16, 2018 at 10:08am PDT 3. Shop floors aren't designed for people in wheelchairs, let's put it that way. Trying to navigate around a shop is no easy feat with clothing rails placed so close together, and it's only made worse when people don’t give you enough space to get through. I end up having to ask my friends to act like some sort of police escort, asking people to move out of the way for me. 4. Sale shopping is stressful for everyone, but when you’re in a wheelchair it’s even worse. With clothes and hangers thrown all over the place by people in a frantic rush, it can be a nightmare. I always end up getting a hanger caught in my wheels and dragging it around the shop while it makes a horrendous scratchy noise across the floor. Cue: people staring, which is always awkward as I try to figure out how to get it out from under my wheels. And I’m not the only one that has issues when shopping on the high-street. Here are some of the experiences other people I know in wheelchairs have had... 5. ""One time I went shopping with my mum and I went into the changing rooms to try on some clothes. But when we got there, the disabled changing rooms were full of stock. We called a member of staff over to get them to move it but they said that it would take too long to move. I ended up not buying the clothes which meant they missed out on a purchase."" - Jenna, @JennaKearnsMusic Ashford dad slams Asda for using disabled changing room as a store cupboard https://t.co/lR2kXXygIB pic.twitter.com/CJEzOYQq0F 6. ""I went to a shop where the womenswear was downstairs. Unfortunately their platform lift was broken so I couldn’t access that floor, but they assured me that it was getting fixed the following week. I live an hour from where the shop was, so I gave it a couple of weeks before going back and it still wasn't fixed. A couple of months later I was back in the area again, and guess what? It still wasn't fixed. I guess accessibility just isn't a priority."" - Marni, @MarniRachel94 7. ""I struggle with having enough space between the clothing racks to get my wheelchair through. I end up getting clothes and coat hangers attached to my chair, which isn’t ideal as it looks like I’m slyly trying to steal things!"" - Sian, @sian_elise17 8. ""When it comes to paying at the checkouts, sometimes they're partitioned off so you have to walk behind someone else who is paying to get to the other cashier. That makes it impossible for someone like me who is a wheelchair user to get through. I usually just sit there awkwardly until one of the cashiers notice me or I have to get my PA to pay and I just wait at the end like a bit of lemon!"" - Eden, @Edenfgk 9. From leaving stretch marks unedited, to encouraging us to embrace our curves and using diverse mannequins that have vitiligo. #InYourOwnSkin is their latest campaign, aiming to celebrate the perceived 'flaws' and 'imperfections' that actually make us who we are. In their commitment to body positivity, Missguided has recruited six women for their latest ad campaign who have scarring, birthmarks, freckles, albinism and other skin conditions. “My role in life is not to be accepted by society. I live fearlessly and I am unapologetically me.” As a plus-size model with albinism, Joanne is dedicated to raising awareness and breaking boundaries in the fashion and beauty industries. “I think we are on the way to empowering women a lot more than we used to. Showing REAL women and not giving everyone the idea that there is just one way to be.” Maya has Epidermolysis Bullosa (EB), a rare condition that affects 5,000 people in the UK. Her goal is to raise awareness of the condition through her modelling work. “Body positivity means being 100% comfortable in yourself, it’s not just the outside but also the inside."" Polly is a full-time model and wants everyone to embrace the concept of women supporting other women. Mariana is a Brazilian model and fashion designer who was born with a birthmark on her face. She hopes to empower others to love the way they look. ""Beauty to me is about what’s inside, personality, happiness, love and acceptance.” Beth has psoriasis and this is her first ever time modelling after Missguided street cast her for the campaign. “Beauty is the feeling of self-confidence."" After being left with scarring across her right arm and back following a house fire when she was 17, Isabella hopes to normalise disabilities and disfigurements through modelling. Missguided we salute you. Follow Laura on Instagram.

" ""I, in no way, was trying to be racist or show cultural appropriation. It was, in fact, cultural appreciation."" Keziah Daum, an 18-year-old high school senior, was looking for a dress to wear to her senior prom and found one at her local vintage store, Decades, in Salt Lake City, Utah. ""I was looking for a dress that was going to be modest in the neckline but also unique,"" she says. ""I’ve always admired the beauty and uniqueness of the Chinese dresses, so I went to that section. I saw that dress, and I was like, ‘OK, this is the dress.’"" But what she chose, a bright, traditional Chinese qipao (or cheongsam) dress, sparked an online debate when she tweeted the photos on April 22, the day after her big night, with the caption ""PROM."" PROM pic.twitter.com/gsJ0LtsCmP One user found the images she posted and wrote a response that went viral, and Daum's photos found their way into a Twitter Moment. My culture is NOT your goddamn prom dress. https://t.co/vhkNOPevKD On prom night, Daum says she received compliments from strangers, waiters at the restaurant she and her friends went to, and teachers, so she was sad and confused when she learned people were offended by her outfit choice. ""I definitely was not expecting it,"" she said. ""I, in no way, was trying to be racist or show cultural appropriation. It was, in fact, cultural appreciation."" Many users came out in support of Daum, while others quickly denounced her dress as cultural appropriation. The qipao, in an early form, was baggy and worn predominantly by upper-class women during the Qing dynasty, which ruled China for more than 250 years until 1912, according to The New York Times. The style then began to merge with Western culture over the decades; it became shorter, featuring slits and tapered waists, evolving into the tight-fitting style that's well-known today. ""At first, I felt bullied, but my mom helped toughen me up, and I began to realise how many people there were who were supporting me in my decision and encouraging me,"" Daum says. ""I learned that there’s always people who are going to hate and I can’t control that."" And while Twitter is in an uproar about her prom dress choice, some people in China are supporting her decision. The story of the Chinese prom dress worn by @daumkeziah that angered a mob of American online activists has reached China. The South China Morning Post reports on how the high schooler is receiving outpouring of support there. https://t.co/mrjcPK1vhC “To Chinese, it’s not sacred and it’s not that meaningful,” said Hung Huang, a Beijing-based writer and fashion blogger, in an interview with The New York Times. Some people took to Weibo, a China-based blogging platform, to write that Daum looked beautiful. “Culture has no borders,"" wrote one user. ""There is no problem, as long as there is no malice or deliberate maligning. Chinese cultural treasures are worth spreading all over the world.” Daum says the controversy hasn't lessened her fun prom-night memories. ""I would, in fact, wear that dress again,"" she says. ""I would buy others like it, because I think it’s a beautiful piece of clothing."" Follow Lauren on Instagram. From: Cosmopolitan US

""After nearly 12 years, my sisters and I have decided to close the doors of our DASH stores,"" Kim wrote in a statement on her website Thursday. ""We opened our first store as a family in 2006 and, since then, we have made so many lifelong memories,"" she continued. ""We've been busy running our own brands, as well as being moms and balancing work with our families. We know in our hearts that it's time to move on."" The sisters opened up their first DASH store in Calabasas, California, in 2006, before their Keeping Up With the Kardashian fame, but later relocated the inaugural store to Los Angeles after the success of their E! reality show. They later opened two more locations in Miami and New York. According to Celebuzz, Khloé wrote in a blog in 2016 about why the sisters decided to open up the stores in the first place. “We started DASH in 2006 and really struggled for a long time to make it a successful business—there were months we couldn’t pay our bills, and the store didn’t turn a profit for years,” Khloé wrote. “After my dad died in 2003, I was partying all the time, drinking a lot and sleeping in every morning. At this time, my mom and Kourtney were running their kids store Smooch, and when the space next door opened up, Kourt got it!” “She saw that I was spiraling and wanted to give me responsibility, a reason to wake up in the morning,"" she continued. ""So, she told me I was going to help her run her new store."" In a Season 13 episode of Keeping Up With the Kardashians, the sisters fought over whether or not to keep the stores open. In the video below, Kim and Khloé were on board to have discussions with potential buyers, but Kourtney really wanted to try and keep the stores open. According to TMZ, the New York store closed down in 2016 due to high rent, so the remaining Los Angeles and Miami locations are the ones being terminated this year. ""We love our DASH Dolls and are so grateful for the amazing memories,"" Kim added in her statement with a mention of the spinoff DASH Dolls, which premiered on E! in 2015. ""And we have to give a special thanks to the DASH employees and all of the incredible fans and customers who have supported us throughout the years! We couldn't have done it without you. Thank you to everyone!"" From: Cosmopolitan US

" It's protocol The royal wedding is getting excitingly close, and so is the due date of Kate Middleton and Prince William's third baby. Despite Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's wedding being mere weeks apart from the birth of the royal baby, the general understanding is that the Duchess of Cambridge will attend the big day. And while we have no idea which designer Kate will choose to wear to the occasion just yet (our money is on Jenny Packham, though!), there is one detail about her royal wedding outfit that we do know. According to The Evening Standard, it is protocol for women attending a royal wedding to wear a hat. And we all know that Kate is a bit more of a stickler for the etiquette rules than Meghan Markle, so we could almost certainly expect her head to be covered on the day. And when we say hat, we don't mean a fascinator, or a hattinator, it has to be a proper, full-on hat. In fact, this is something that all guests attending the royal wedding should take note of, as Anglican Church rules require women to cover their heads inside the church. So, while we still don't know what Meghan Markle will be wearing, we can expect to see a lot of exciting headgear heading into the church on May the 19th.

""I was very lucky that the first agency I was with actually discovered me through Instagram. They found me because I commented on one of Iskra Lawrence’s posts. I had been following her for a while and she posted something about body positivity, so I just commented something like ‘you look great girl’ and that’s how my agent found me. My profile was private but she followed me and then direct messaged me the next day asking if I was interested in modelling. I really thought it was a scam at first because unless watching a lot of America's Next Top Model counts, I had never done any modelling before. The @allwomanproject asked women to talk about which part of their body they've grown to love. For me, it's being a curvy girl. It's been a rollercoaster. For most of my life, being curvy wasn't something to be proud of. You were expected to diet your way to a slim figure. I've always been this girl with curves, hips, and a booty. It comes with being Latina. I used to dread going to the beach and wearing a bikini. My tummy always rolled. My thighs always chaffed when walking on the pier. It took me way too many summer days hiding away under a beach umbrella and covered up to realize that my body is beautiful and I should be as confident as any other girl on the beach. Now I celebrate the skin I'm in. 💦 #iamallwoman #morethanamodel A post shared by Bella Golden (@bellaagolden) on Feb 28, 2017 at 10:53am PST ""When I was first scouted I was working at Disneyland California as a character performer, which is kind of funny when I think back because I guess I've been posing for pictures longer than I realised. When people found out I worked at Disneyland they would always ask me if I was a Princess but I wasn't. I was the one dressed in a full on animal suit completely sweating."" 💚✨ A post shared by Bella Golden (@bellaagolden) on Sep 9, 2017 at 9:53am PDT ""People ask me 'how are you plus-size?', or 'it’s terrible you’re considered plus-size' but I don’t take it as a bad thing. In fashion if you’re over a size 4 (UK size 8) you’re considered plus-size, that's the crazy thing. I’m a size 12 (UK size 16) but when I’m shopping online I realise from looking at the size guides and measurements, I never fit in one box. I think fashion designers expect people to be a perfect hourglass shape but who actually fits that? I can go from a size 8 (UK size 12) in one brand to a size 14 (UK size 18) in another, but I think every girl has that struggle. So although I don't have a problem being labelled as plus-size, I do think the term is problematic in a sense because I don't like the idea of separation, that one group of people is superior to another. feelin free, liberated, beautiful and powerful ✨ reminder: you're so beautiful and uniquely you. don't let anyone dull or dumb you down. surround yourself with people who empower you and make you feel important. treat yourself kindly and don't compare yourself.
