" Summer, come at me. With news of a record-breaking heatwave fast-approaching, the question of what to wear to work in summer becomes somewhat time critical. Whilst we might've scraped by this season so far with the same midi dress and sneaker combo, the looming threat of three consecutive days above thirty degrees has us looking for more office-appropriate options. From zesty colour ideas to snazzy dress inspo, here's the 2019 guide to the best summer fashion trends you can wear to work when it's hot outside... The trouser suit is an office wardrobe staple. Add some seasonal zing to the look by choosing for a set in sweet sorbet hues. If you're feeling extra keen, why not team your co-ords with contrasting colour accessories like a headband or handbag? Accessorising is one of the easiest hacks for updating your outfit to fit the season. And this summer the 'more is more' mantra rings truer than ever. Layer your gold chain necklaces, add a pair of luxe hoop earrings and stack your rings all the way to the top. Your pretty day dresses are practically made for the summer work environment. Elevate the look by adding a sophisticated blazer over the top, matching shades and a pair of minimalist strappy sandals for extra style points. Keep the back of your neck cool by tying your hair up. Make like the fashion kids by selecting an on-trend printed or textured scrunchie. Tie dye is back, folks. While we wouldn't necessarily recommend wearing a full-on hippy dress to your important meeting - unless, of course, you really want to - add a little nod to the trend into your outfit with quirky accessories like technicolour handbags and silk scarves. Who said bike shorts aren't work appropriate? Answer: practically everyone. Granted, you might not be able to get away with this one at every office, but if you're in a more creative field, this is a fresh take on the ol' short suit. You really can't go wrong with a fun maxi dress. Team with a pair of low heels that are easy to walk in and a matching bag and you're good to go! Nothing screams summer more than a raffia bag. Keep the work appropriate vibes by selecting mini, top-handle styles (as opposed to your massive beach bag), et voila! While wearing one colour might feel like a bold fashion move (and it kinda is) it's also a super easy way to instantly elevate your outfit. If you're not feeling brave enough to start with 100% saturated tones, try pastel hues instead and work your way up. Monochrome is also a fail-safe office classic. Add some summer vibes by switching out your blouse for a sleeveless number, sandals and a contrasting bag. Slouchy suits have been one of this season's most coveted trends. Take the look into summer by swapping out your wide-leg trousers for a paid of boxy shorts and BOOM! You're donezo. When it's hot outside, a mini dress is the first thing you want to reach for. And there's a simple way to take your evening dresses to the office. Simply grab your looser fitted pieces and team them with summery jewellery and your favourite leather bag. Metallic is a summer mainstay for a reason. It's fresh, crisp and can instantly take any outfit from 'cool' to 'damn chic'. These pants are a neat example if you feel like going all-out, but a silver pair of pumps or bag will work just as well. Whether you're using them to make a mismatch suit, or simply to elevate one of your favourite logo tees, the wide-leg palazzo pants are back in style. Make sure to opt for long legs that scrunch at the ankle, and tapered pleats around the waist for the most flattering fit. Much like the bike short suggestion, only some places are chill with you wearing shorts to the office. If you fancy giving your denim piece a try, your best bet is to match the with a freshly ironed collared shirt and preppy blazer that sits lower than the hemline on your shorts.

" ""Stop wearing/using the product immediately. Keep away from children"" River Island is recalling five clothing items after fears they contain harmful levels of the chemicals Lead and Cadmium. The high street retailer has issued a public notice including pictures of the clothes in question (available in store and online since February 2018) on its website. ""Stop wearing/using the product immediately. Keep away from children. Return the whole product to us in store or post them to us for a full refund inclusive of postage"" writes the brand. The first batch of clothes being recalled includes two check pattern pieces, a dress (Product no. 723969) and a sleeveless blouse (Product no. 723975) style, with white collars and faux pearl details, both sold from July 2018. ""It has come to our attention that the faux pearl button located on the collars of both products contain Cadmium in excess of legal safety levels and presents a serious risk to the health of anyone wearing or handling the products,"" writes River Island. ""Affected products can be identified by the product identification numbers printed on the garments wash care label."" The second batch features three embellished items: a tassel playsuit (Product no. 714210), sequin embellished cami top (Product no. 720271) and longline diamante studded hoody in cream (Product no. 725642), sold in store and online from February 2018. ""It has come to our attention that the components on each product identified above contain Lead in excess of legal safety levels and presents a serious risk to the health of anyone wearing or handling the products. Affected products can be identified by the product identification numbers printed on the garments wash care label."" It's important to see as some high-fashion brands still struggle to embrace bigger sizes on the runway and in ads. Inclusivity is a constant theme in Rihanna's brands. She launched Fenty Beauty with 40 shades of foundation, which especially benefitted people of colour who've often had limited options of darker cosmetic shades to choose from. She included a plus-size collection in her Savage x Fenty lingerie line and featured models of various body sizes (including two pregnant women) in the runway show. The size representation does not stop with her Fenty fashion line, which goes up to the French size 46 (size 18 in the UK). ""We have our fit models, which is the standard size from factories, you just get your samples made in one size,"" Rihanna explained to E! News at the pop-up launch. ""But then, I want to see it on my body, I want to see it on a curvy girl with thighs and a little bit of booty and hips."" ""It's all of these things I take into consideration because I want women to feel confident in my stuff,"" she added. Size diversity is just as impactful for consumers to see on mannequins as it is on runway models and actual clothes. Racked reported in 2017 that mannequins are the ""strongest method of 'silent selling'"" and one that ""looks or is shaped like like the customer"" is more likely to influence sales. As The Guardian reported in 2015, the average mannequin has the following unrealistic measurements: six-foot height, 34-inch bust, 24-inch waist, and 34-inch hips. Penny and David's Bridal have already done so, according to Racked, and Nordstrom and Target are adding shapelier mannequins to their stores, The Wall Street Journal reports. " One bad experience can scar you for life. Have you noticed how clothes shops are rigidly gendered? Well, as a non-binary person, you really do. Non-binary people self-identify, essentially making our own rules on our identity and gender which can make shopping anything from tricky to traumatic. I cannot tell you how many times I have been turned away from changing rooms for one reason or another. During one memorable trip to M&S, I went to the female changing room to try on some clothes from the women's section. They quickly directed me to the men's changing room, where I was then helpfully told I wasn't allowed to try on female clothes. At that moment, I felt so vulnerable and embarrassed that I simply left. Now, I will not try clothes on in the shops for fear of judgement - I prefer to buy and try on at home. There are a few exceptions to the rule though, such as H&M's all gender changing rooms, and recently I have used Zara changing rooms without issue. Whether it's a double take or a full look up and down, it can be uncomfortable to feel as though you are ALWAYS being watched. Luckily, I am now in a place where I'm completely comfortable with who I am, and can ignore that unwanted attention. In fact, I'll happily stare right back at Carol and Susan whilst flicking through the blouses in M&S. Okay, so I've learnt to shrug off the stares, but sometimes, someone will openly comment on my presence, which is harder to deal with. Things I’ve heard in the past include: ‘What is that?!’, ‘God only knows what your parents think of you’, ‘What have you come as today?!’ and ‘Don’t you want to be normal?’. In most circumstances I just smile at their ignorance and remember I’m worth so much more than their opinion. When I walk though a store, I always notice the way the way staff react, or don’t react to me. I’ll be looking for something, and they will blatantly ignore me, or I’ll catch somebody’s eye and they will avert their gaze. To me, it's like they are suggesting that I shouldn’t be there, which feels worse than the response from customers, because the staff are paid to help me. Nearly all shops have gendered departments in their stores; Women’s and Men’s. When presented with a binary store layout, it forces you to define your gender, and thus your choices, which is the antithesis of being non-binary. I wear clothes from all departments, so if I am shopping for jeans, I have twice as much choice (amazing) but have to cover twice as much floor space (not so amazing). Not only is it confusing in terms of identity, but it’s really tiring, Ms Bradshaw was right in SATC when she said that shopping was her cardio. Realistically, for things that I can access in both male and female departments, I shop online from the comfort of my safe space (read bed). It is unrealistic to expect all high street stores to advertise its clothing on all genders. However, when faced with so much gender-specific marketing, it can affect how you feel about certain garments, leading you to second guess yourself. As a non-binary person, I shop in all sections as it allows me to express myself in the way I want. But with so much variety when it comes to sizing, from store to store, item to item, department to department, finding the right fit can be very confusing. It makes shopping for the perfect jumpsuit a living nightmare. So you’ve worked out your size, and what you are looking for, now you have to deal with the fact that the store you are in doesn’t have what you want. I have size 11 feet and sometimes would like to wear heels. The only store that goes anywhere near my size in heels is New Look, where I wear a wide fit in a U.K. 9 and still end up crushing my toes. Thankfully brands that cater to larger feet, such as Tskenya and Syro are becoming more prevalent. I’m not being dramatic when I say that one bad shopping experience can scar you for life. Re-entering a shop can make you feel like a glutton for punishment. There are several places that I've avoided for years, due to mis-gendering and refusal of store services. Now, I try and shop with friends or family to take the pressure off me, or I shop in places I know to be more accepting, which isn’t always easy. My favourite places to shop are ASOS (I love their new Collusion range), Zara and H&M. Shop now ASOS Collusion Follow Ben on Instagram.

I realised I was lying about the reality of it, so I decided I was going to say it how it is. I’m so glad I did. I had so many messages, so many people reaching out to me. It was like a weight had been lifted off my shoulders. I’d been feeling like a fraud, so to be honest it felt really good."" ""I get it every day! Although I come across as a confident person, I still get moments of real self-doubt. I’ll worry endlessly that I’m getting something wrong. Like everyone, I get scared about all the 'what ifs'. But I’ve realised that you have to get out of your head. You don’t know something will go wrong until you try. If it works it works; if it doesn’t work, you learn. I’m trying to be more decisive and not let my inner critic overthink things."" ""People often ask me how to have the confidence to dress or style themselves a bit differently to the norm. It’s simple really: just do it. You don’t have to explain yourself to anybody. If you don’t want to wear makeup, don’t. If you want to colour your hair, do it! If you’re a guy that wants to wear womenswear, no one has a right to judge you, and if they do, they don’t matter. Just do you. " #7 is genius if your zip won't stay up. Broken zippers are arguably the most awkward fashion piece to fix because, the more you try and move the slider up and down (in various states of stress), the more broken the zip can often become. While you often take a bung zipper to your local alterations shop for a replacement, if you're on your way out and your dress or bag suddenly break on you, you want a quick and simple solution. Here we round up the best zipper repair tricks using household items such as Vaseline, a pencil and even nail polish. Scroll down for easy, fast solutions to get you on your way again. When your zipper is broken, there could be multiple reasons why. First, let's make sure we know the names for each part of a zip (including the teeth, slider and puller) so the instructions are as clear as possible: 1. Use pliers Does your zipper seem to work properly but then, as soon as it's fastened, all the teeth come undone? The problem is the slider, AKA - the piece that's meant to lock the teeth together. Over time, these sliders start to loosen and gape, which makes they become less effective at binding the teeth in place. While you can take your garment to a tailor to replace the entire zipper, there is a simple, more affordable hack you can try first. While the slider is still attached to the garment, reach for a pair of pliers. The part of the slider that attaches to the puller (on the outwards facing side of garment), is called the top plate. The part of the slider that faces in inwards side of the garment is then called the bottom plate. Use your tweezers to squeeze the top and bottom plate together to help restore the slider to its original, tighter shape. An easy way to gauge is to check that the gap between the two places (where there teeth live) is getting smaller. Be careful not to press too hard at once, in case it breaks the slider. The aim is to do this gradually in multiple steps, compressing the plates on either side of the puller until it's right. Watch this video to see the full process: 2. Grab a screwdriver If one or both sides of the slider come off the teeth, the zipper doesn't necessarily need replacing, the slide just needs reattaching. To do this, you first need to find the 'bottom' of the zip. The bottom of the zip is, typically, the end closest to the floor when you're wearing the garment. If you can't tell which is the right side, look for the end with a square tab of fabric after the zip finishes. Then, feed the teeth from that end into the slider. If you need extra leverage to push the teeth into place, use a flathead screwdriver. Once the teeth are in both sides of the slider, use the puller to move it up and down the track to lock it in place. 3. Use tweezers First, check to see if there's anything caught in the zip, like another garment or even rogue fibres. If possible, remove these obstructions by hand before retrying the zip. If, however, the stuck item/s won't move, try going in with a pair of tweezers to slowly pull the blockage out of the teeth. Sometimes softly wiggling the puller up and down as you tug on the slider can also help dislodge tougher items. 4. Use a pencil or washing up liquid If the zip still won't move, you might need to give it a little extra help. Start by using a pencil to coat the teeth surrounding the lodge with a light coating of graphite - this will act as a lubricant to help facilitate a smooth run. If that fails, try a small amount of washing up liquid, to further aid the slider move up and down the teeth. 5. Try Vaseline If the pencil and washing up liquid don't work, or if you're worried they might stain your clothing, try Vaseline instead. Start by reaching for a cotton bud, coating the outside of the bud with a light layer of Vaseline. Then, use the bud to work the jelly into the teeth surrounding the stoppage. The idea is that the Vaseline will help remove any smaller items that may be stuck in the zip. Zippers that are missing teeth can be particularly fiddly to fix so we recommend taking your garment to a tailored to repair this specific issue. In the meantime, scroll down to see our quick fixes until you have time to get to the alterations shop. 6. Use pliers If your zip keeps falling down, it often means that the teeth have either been dislodged or worn away. Start by closely inspecting the zip itself to determine if any of the teeth might be simple out are out of alignment. If so, use a set of pliers to slowly bend the rogue teeth back into position. Alternatively, if they all appear to be in the correct place, move onto the next step. 7. Try nail polish If you suspect the teeth have worn down from too much use, a trick that might work is painting the teeth with clear nail polish. This will effectively thicken the teeth, potentially restoring your zip to its former working glory. If you find that the zip still doesn't fasten after your first coat of polish it might be that they need another coat or two. Note: making sure to allow enough time for each layer to dry properly before going in over the top with another coat, otherwise the teeth with become sticky and rough. 8. Use a paper clip If all else fails and you can't seem to get the pesky zip to stay in place, you might need to replace the zipper entirely. Until then, a short term fix involves feeding a paper clip into this loop on the slider: Then, hook the other side of the paper clip over the button or clasp as the top of the zipper to hold the whole thing in place. 9. Or a safety pin Alternatively, if you have a safety pin handy, simple pin either side of the zip closed, like this: These aren't long term solutions, but can come in super handy if your zip breaks while you're out and about or if you don't have time to get them repaired. 10. Don't yank it The best way to prevent breaking your zipper is by making sure you don't use too much force. Instead, use steady, consistent pulls to guide the sliders up and down the zip. 11. Make sure the zip is not under too much pressure If you're trying fasten a bag that's overflowing or jeans that are too small, it's entirely possible the zip will buckle if there's too much pressure pulling the teeth apart. The trick here is avoid forcing the zip. When there's a significant amount of resistance sliding the zipper closed this is often a sign that, even if you manage to close it, the zip will subsequently break.

" It'll call you an Uber, too. It was only a matter of time before someone invented a smart handbag. Today, Tracey Hummel officially debuted her luxury handbag label Bee & Kin, fusing two seemingly different worlds—fashion and tech—together. Her bags (there are five distinct styles along with tiny pouches) are all equipped with two unique buttons: a built-in flashlight and a button that connects to your phone. It's the second that's pretty genius. Via your phone's bluetooth, the bag's smart button connects to an app called Flic, which you use to program all the various functions you want your button to be able to execute, like ordering an Uber or sending a text message. It can also make your phone ring, which means you can now get away from that bad date without begging your bestie to call you with a fake emergency halfway through. The luxury bags range from £400 to £570 and, while they are driven by tech, they still feel feminine and wearable to fashion lovers. Growing up, Hummel always had one foot in tech (her dad worked in the space and she studied a mix of entrepreneurship and computer information systems in college) and one foot in fashion, specifically production and design. Prior to launching her own brand, she worked at Tory Burch as a production assistant. ""Ever since I was a little girl [designing my own handbags] was what I wanted to do,"" Hummels says. ""After college, I went into the fashion/corporate world to get a better understanding of how everything worked in order to eventually bring my brand, Bee & Kin, to life."" In fact, two of the bags in her line, the sidekick and hero tote, were the very first designs she sketched back in high school. ""It's so exciting to have those come to life after many years,"" she shares. Having let those ideas simmer for so long, it's clear everything Hummel does is intentional, not accidental—from the bag's smart buttons to its structural design and spandex lining (to protect your gear) to even the brand's name: Her last name, Hummel, when translated from German, means bumblebee. All the accessories feature a hexagon shape—a honeycomb, if you will. ""This is all pretty much a nod to my heritage and upbringing,"" she says. ""The honeycomb is a reminder of my family's hardworking background."" Hummel wanted to include a light in the bag from the start. ""I was going to and from work and constantly looking in my bag for an Oyster card,"" she recalls. ""I would dig for 10 minutes and people are like, 'Are you good?' I’m like, ""I’m great, just looking for something in my bag,"" she laughs. From there, the brand wanted to show the breadth of fashion and function by incorporating the shortcuts. Hummel says they're even currently working on some prototypes that integrate a sleek, luxurious wireless phone charger into the bag. But does it work? I had the opportunity to test out one of Hummel's Bee & Kin bags before the launch to see exactly how helpful the smart button was in my everyday life. I chose the expert tote in black since it seemed the best for work. After downloading the Flic app—which was free and easy to install, plus intuitive to use—I added the functions I wanted my tote bag's smart button to do. There were many dozens functions to choose from, which were broken up into categories including fitness, phone control, media, and games. Two quick FYIs: I discovered your bluetooth has to be on at all times, so the bag's smart button can be connected to your Flic app. Some features, like share your location, cost Flic credits (which you pay for) because it uses a third-party SMS service—a slight bummer. Still, several of the functions were free and quite useful; other's not as much. I am always misplacing my phone, so this was one feature I was eager to try. When I'm in a hurry to leave the house and don't know where my phone is, I go to my bag, press the smart button and wait for a sound to go off (it sounds like an alarm). The noise makes it super easy to locate your phone. This feature can double as your ""escape a bad date"" false ringtone. (On Android devices, there's actually an escape a bad date function in the Flic app, which you can pair to your bag's smart button. That feature is coming for iPhones.) This is helpful when you're in a car or doing something that requires your undivided attention. You can easily reach into your bag and double tap the button to hang up incoming calls without ever picking up your phone. The Uber function was finicky for me—after a week, it still won't connect to my app—but I like the idea of being able to call a car by clicking a button in my tote bag. The brand is currently working with Flic to improve user function. FYI: You have to preset your pick-up and drop-off location in the Flic app first. As long as you have your camera app open in the background of your iPhone, you can hold the bag's smart button down and it'll automatically snap a photo for you. Though this was not a feature I used regularly, I could see it being useful if you're trying to take a group photo or something. From: Marie Claire US

" This is SO interesting. Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex (AKA Meghan Markle) and Catherine, the Duchess of Cambridge (Kate Middleton) both have undeniable fashion influence. But have you ever wondered who has the bigger fashion influence out of Meghan and Kate - y'know, out of curiosity? This sounds like a hard thing to gauge but, thanks to the internet, it turns out there's a pretty logical way to measure it. Every year UK fashion retailer Lyst trawls through its search data to find a handful of juicy insights. Most recently, the brand analysed 20 million search enquiries relating to the Duchess' fashion choices over the last two years and found that one woman came out nearly twice as popular as the other in terms of search. The findings revealed that Meghan's outfits have nearly double the amount of online interest compared to Kate's. This year alone, Meghan's style has prompted a 216 per cent increase in search on average, whereas Kate's still had a sizeable (albeit comparatively less) 119 percent increase. The report went on to state that Meghan's outfit choices tend to influence colour trends, while Kate's spark interest in specific designers. For example, when Meghan made her first appearance after giving birth to baby Archie, searches for her 'white trench dress' went up 46 per cent in the following 12 hours. Conversely, when Kate stepped out at the Commonwealth Day celebrations wearing a red Catherine Walker coat dress, searches for similar styles went up 225 per cent. Interesting huh? While there might be a numerical difference in what people are searching, we love the Duchesses (and their respective styles) equally.

" Fresh #OOTDs, minus the high street haul? Challenge accepted. I am not an influencer. The fact that I only have a few hundred followers is proof of that. However, if you happen to be one of them, you might think that I think I’m an influencer – judging by the pure volume of mirror selfies, OOTDs and #candid laughing pics. I can see where you might be confused. In actuality, Instagram is just something I do for fun. Partly because I enjoy the fact that my mum often comments on my posts: ‘Looking good, sweetie!’ I don’t care how old you are, we all still want a bit of validation from our mums. I also find that posting pictures of my outfits pushes me to be a bit more creative with my style. You don’t get likes with repeats, so the pressure is on to come up with new looks. Often that involves ASOS hauls and high street sprees. I’m certainly guilty of falling victim to fast fashion. But I also know that nonstop shopping is pretty terrible for the environment (and my bank account). So, I teamed up with Comfort and challenged myself to wear five new outfits without buying anything. If I deemed them OOTD-worthy, I’d consider the experiment a success. So, how did I manage to pull together new outfits without typing in my card details? Thankfully I didn’t resort to shoplifting. Instead, I tried a few resourceful tactics... I wore old clothes in a new way For outfit one, I dug out an ASOS dress that I bought several months ago but had only worn once. Because of the high neck and ruffles, it felt a little too twee when I first wore it to work. But, inspired to try something new, I removed the slip dress underneath and wore the sheer outer layer over jeans and a cami top. To add to the theme, I paired it with high heels that I hadn’t worn in about three years because, lately, wearing heels just feels like too much effort. I really liked this outfit – it definitely felt cooler this way. But I got the most compliments on the shoes. Maybe I should rotate some heels back into my workwear every now and then? I shopped my husband's wardrobe Often when you think of 'borrowing from the boys', you picture oversized shirts belted at the waist or baggy jeans rolled up. But my husband, Paul, and I are pretty much the exact same size – right down to the shoes. This fact made the challenge a bit easier... and also made me wonder why I don’t do this more often. For day two, I wore Paul's striped shirt, mustard Reebok trainers and one of his ties as a choker. I did wear my own trousers, but three out of four isn’t bad! I got a few compliments on this look at the office, but for the most part no one clocked that it was anything out of the ordinary. And they were all shocked when I revealed that I was wearing his shoes. (You might think I’d be embarrassed to reveal that fact publicly, but here we are.) For my third outfit, I dipped into his polo collection. When I say this guy loves a polo shirt, I mean he loves a polo shirt. I don’t think I’ve worn one since I went through a super preppy phase in 2007 – but, in the name of journalism, I got stuck in.In order to make it look a little less ‘American frat boy’, I paired it with a sequin skirt, which I’ve only ever worn when going ‘out out.’ So this definitely qualified as old clothes in a new way. I finished off the look with Paul’s white Lacoste trainers.This look got the most comments by far, but I’m not sure I would class them as compliments. It was more along the lines of: 'Wow, that’s a look'. Or, 'You look shiny!' Or my favourite: 'That skirt is loud!' (Meant literally. It made a somewhat ridiculous clanking sound when I walked.) In hindsight, it may not have been the most practical work outfit. But it definitely looked good on the 'gram! I swapped with my BFF One thing I miss most about living with my girlfriends is sharing clothes. In my university days, I could shout a request for a black top down the hall and immediately be presented with at least five options: tube, halter, cowl neck, handkerchief, lingerie-inspired. (RIP, 2000s fashion.) So for my last trick, I texted one of my closest friends and requested a trade. It turns out the actual swapping part was the best bit. Kiley and I drank wine, rummaged through her wardrobe and chatted about our weekend plans. And I left with a tote bag of options for new looks. The challenge week happened to include my mini-break in Italy, so I was looking for clothes I could bring with me. And Kiley happens to be about two sizes smaller than me (and eight inches shorter), so finding clothes that would work was tricky. In the end I went for kimonos and floaty dresses that fit my seaside vibe – and my body. For my fourth outfit, I wore a vintage yellow lace dress of hers over a swimsuit. I hardly ever shop vintage because it's so hit or miss, and I find fit to be a challenge. But I absolutely fell in love with this piece. It was perfect as a cover-up, if not entirely practical (I wouldn’t dare get it wet!). And the bright colour made for the ideal OOTD. For my final outfit, I wore a silk kimono of Kiley's (vintage again), belted over a slip dress of mine (that I’ve never worn because it’s slightly too tight on my hips). Paired with red block-heeled sandals, it was the perfect look for dinner on the water. And, of course, to make the swap fair, it had to go both ways. I was so pleased to see Kiley wear a co-ord set of mine to a wedding – the ultimate stamp of approval! If you fancy swapping on a bigger level, why not join us for the Cosmopolitan Swap Shop, in partnership with Comfort and The Prince’s Trust? You can breathe new life into your wardrobe and you'll be doing your bit for charity. THE VERDICT Pulling together five new, 'gram-worthy looks without spending any money wasn’t easy, but it was certainly a success. The challenge forced me to get creative with my styling and pushed me out of my comfort zone. Next time I find myself reaching for my credit card, I just might go rummage through my husband’s wardrobe, instead. Guard your trainers, Paul! Discover the positive power of clothes with Comfort

" An investigation. You might have heard—the Trumps have touched down in London for their official UK state visit. One of their very first stops is, of course, to see Queen Elizabeth and the rest of the royal family, and on Monday night they all enjoyed a banquet together. The banquet is being held at Buckingham Palace, and is being attended by around 150 guests, including Prince Charles, Prince William, and Kate Middleton. Prince Charles and Camilla were one of the firsts to greet President Donald Trump and Melania, along with Queen Elizabeth, and they all took a photo in the ballroom of Buckingham Palace. The group all wore coordinating white outfits, with the men in black-and-white tuxes while the women all wore white dresses. Melania paired her floor-length gown with white gloves, as did the Queen herself. Kate Middleton was later spotted on her way to the event, also wearing a white Alexander McQueen dress. It's interesting to note that all the women decided to rock the neutral hue, as the dress code for the white-tie affair did not specify that one had wear all white. Traditionally, white tie just calls for women to be in a long gown, while men should be in a full tuxedo including a white bow tie. (For example, Birgitte, Duchess of Gloucester, and British PM Theresa May wore blue and black, respectively.) Perhaps the royals coordinated with Melania Trump on wearing white as a courteous move? After all, the colour is smart and elegant for formal affairs. ""I agree it would appear as if there was an agreement that all the royal woman would wear white and Melania was advised to do the same, but I really think it is a coincidence,"" said MarieClaire.com's exclusive royal wedding expert and British bridal designer, Caroline Castigliano. ""The royals often wear white to the state banquets and I wonder if this is partly to show off their sashes. Kate wore her blue sash tonight for the first time that symbolises her role as a member of the Royal Victorian Order."" The irony of everyone wearing all white isn't lost on political watchers; the color has been used by different groups as a form of protest. During President Trump's State of Union address in February, many Democratic congresswomen wore white, the color adopted by the suffragist movement, to pay homage to that and their fight for women's rights. (The Trump administration is currently threatening the very existence of Roe v. Wade.) In addition, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made a sartorial statement by wearing a white suit to her 116th Congress swearing-in ceremony. And going even further back, Hillary Clinton wore white to Trump's inauguration. It should be noted that the Obamas also wore white when they attended a state banquet with the Queen in 2011...so maybe everyone just loves this hue for royal parties? Counterpoint: Melania and Camilla also wore white for a daytime excursion prior to the banquet itself. From: Marie Claire US

" Including what not to do As impractical as suede shoes may be, we can't help having a strong sartorial affinity for them. They're versatile, classy and, more often than not, super comfortable - just ask Elvis Presley. What we don't like, however, is when they (inevitably) get dirty and need cleaning. But how do you clean something that can't even get wet? Here are four easy steps for quickly and effectively cleaning suede boots, trainers, heels and sandals. If you don't have a suede brush, a clean nail brush or tooth brush will work just fine. Begin by using light strokes to brush the surface of the shoe to remove loose particles and grit. When brushing, remember to brush with the grain (AKA, in the same direction the suede naturally sits). For more stubborn marks, like scuff marks, apply more pressure and move the brush in a swift back and forth direction to help raise flattened suede fibres, to further aid with cleaning. If the dirt is still wet, wipe off the excess and leave to dry before removing the particles with a brush. If you try cleaning the stain why it's still damp, it can often work the particles deeper into the suede, making it harder to remove in the long run. If you have a suede rubber, that's even better, but your regular pencil-case version will still work well, providing the rubber has been buffed free of any pre-existing stains first. Think of this as a slightly more rigorous approach for clearing scuff marks, by using constant, back and forth pressure to help dislodge any surplus particles. While applying a liquid like white vinegar might seem counter-intuitive, it's acidic composition means it's brilliant at breaking down particles clumps - which is exactly what you want for cleaning. Dip the corner of your flannel/face washer into a small bowl of vinegar (be careful not to drench the entire cloth) before applying to the stain and rubbing in a back and forth motion. Keep working at the mark and reapplying vinegar where necessary to effectively remove the station. The key with this step is repetition and patience. Note: The vinegar will temporarily dampen the suede, altering the colour of the fabric, before evaporating and returning the fabric to its original colour. To determine if the stain has been properly removed, you might need to use multiple applications of vinegar and drying. The age-old saying 'prevention is better than cure' certainly rings true with suede shoes. But not all suede protectors are made equal. Reviews often cite permanent colour changes when using particular products so, if you intend on using a protector, the best approach is to base your selection off customer ratings and reviews to avoid any unwanted results. " Either way, it's fire. When the Duchess of Cambridge, Kate Middleton, stepped out at Bletchley Park earlier this week wearing her breathtaking Alessandra Rich polka dot dress, we all stopped and had to take a second to scoop our jaws back up off the floor. I mean, could she look any more flawless? Nope. On closer inspection, however, this dress turned out to be a lot more than just pretty - it was also unconventional. The calf-grazing navy blue number, with a contrasting white collar, long sleeves and button-up detailing inadvertently seemed to break royal fashion protocol. As antiquated as the idea of 'royal fashion protocol' might sound, there are a lot of things that Duchess Kate and her new sister-in-law, Meghan Markle, are expected to adhere to. And they do, for the most part. But when these women occasionally decide to break away from what's considered 'traditional' or 'conventional' royal style, a big part of us can't help yelling 'YAS!!!'. So how did Kate's polka dot dress break convention, you ask? Well, it's all to do with the front split. When the royal was standing inside, the dress effortlessly sits in the one place. But when the Duchess made her way around outside, the cross-wind revealed a super high (and 3000% fierce) leg split. A quick FYI: It's customary for royal women to wear under-the-knee dresses and skirts. Similarly, if the piece is made from a lighter material, small weights are often added to the hemline to keep the garment in place. I have to admit, the high-cut detail makes me love this spotty dress even more - something I didn't think was even possible, but here we are. Now, if you cast your mind back to late last year, you might also recall Meghan receiving similar coverage about breaking 'royal style rules', when she stepped out in Fraser Island (during her first royal tour with Prince Harry) wearing a maxi dress with a thigh-high split. Here's the dress in question: When you zoom in on Meghan's dress, you can see a mini fastening attached at the top of the split (presumably sewn on by the designer or the Duchess' stylist) to prevent any potential wardrobe malfunctions. Notably, this detail wasn't added to Kate's dress. And since we find it hard to believe that there wasn't as much thought put into the duchess' outfit, it's very possible that this might've been a conscious decision to leave the polka dot number unstitched and unweighted. Thank you for listening to my Ted Talk.

For the uninitiated, 'slozy' was a term originally coined by Racked back in 2017, and refers to the hybrid of 'slutty' and 'cozy' outfits.* The look should also include ""an element made of the softest jersey or velour of faux fur imaginable"" - y'know, all the name of comfort. *While I have to admit I really don't like the word 'slutty', in this instance, the internet is using it interchangeably with 'sexy', the second of which I'm very in favour of. This viral trend all started when one user recently wrote that she'd discovered a term perfectly describing a style she' s never been able to articulate before. The thread has now been upvoted over two thousands times and received a tonne of comments from other individuals who feel the same way. The user defined 'slozy' fashion in her own words: Other users also jumped in with their own terms for this particular aesthetic. My personal favourites include 'sexy Grandma' along with 'tits and knits'. The original Racked article describes the two steps to 'slozy dressing'. First, start by thinking of the body part/s that you like about yourself and want to accentuate in your outfit. Next, reach for comfortable items in your wardrobe that draw the eye to those said areas. For example, if you really like your shoulders and décolletage area, try opting for a slouchy jumper with a lacy bralette poking out. Alternatively, if you're all about your legs, your look might be a mini knit dress with thigh-high boots. " Anything is possible if you just believe Leggings are one of those wardrobe pieces that are as brilliant as they are dangerous. The first part is obvious - they’re comfortable and oh-so-easy to put on for a gym class, a quick trip to the shops, or even out and about as you tick off your to-do list... which brings us to the second part. The downfall of leggings is that they are so comfortable that it’s not long before you find that you’re wearing them 24/7. And whilst they have many redeeming qualities, I think we can all agree that they’re probably not the best looking trousers in your wardrobe. As a result, the question we find ourselves asking is as much 'how to wear leggings?’ as ‘should I wear leggings?’. We’re looking to bridge that gap by offering stylish ways to wear your beloved elasticated bottoms to a slew of different occasions, all while looking fashionable as heck.
